data.brief: The endgame isn't replacing model judgment but flooring it: every deterministic function added is "more reliable ground for the LLM to stand on" (their "1.1.0 tools" framing) — develop with software 3.0, productionize by adding software 1.0 for the use cases that earn it
data.name: Deterministic functions are reliable ground for the LLM to stand on

data.brief: Moving to ML changed everything about the stack — probabilistic behavior ("correct is a distribution"), copyable weights leaking through the serving API, shared multi-tenant GPUs, prompts as control flow — but nobody changed the security assumptions: we run a 2008 playbook on a 2026 system. The fix is the boring one: secure the LLM stack like a database — lock down access, segment the network, protect data at rest
data.name: We run a 2008 security playbook on a 2026 ML system

data.brief: 2026 is the adoption year; 2027 the conversation shifts to governance — can you trust shipped code, who is accountable when an AI-authored change causes an incident, where is the audit trail; a review-debt number is the bridge that lets teams have the governance conversation without abandoning the throughput gains
data.name: 2026 is the adoption year; 2027 shifts the conversation to governance

data.brief: Gain generalizes past this benchmark into the discipline the memory-product category currently lacks: run the system twice, once with state and once with state wiped, and report the delta. Almost no memory or context-management product is evaluated this way, which is precisely why a category can grow without demonstrating that its machinery beats simply putting the experience in the context. The stateless control arm is cheap, obvious in retrospect, and would settle most vendor claims in this space — which is a reasonable definition of a good metric
data.name: A stateless control arm for memory

data.brief: Codebase abstraction is the architecture of auto-research: it sets constraints and priors, and the starting point hugely biases the whole search direction. A good abstraction steers agents toward solutions that generalize — and makes reward hacking structurally hard — even when scores look identical
data.name: Codebase abstraction is the architecture of auto-research

data.brief: Headline agent-capability curves are quoted at 50% success; at enterprise-grade accuracy the effective task horizon collapses ~5× — the exponential is real, but "enterprise grade" lives on the much flatter 80%-accuracy curve
data.name: At enterprise-grade accuracy the effective task horizon collapses ~5x

data.brief: Accessibility and challenge stop being separate concerns and become two ends of one continuously-tuned dial; a live layout auditor adapts the game to the human in real time rather than forcing the human to adapt to fixed menus — turning devices into responsive, empathetic partners
data.name: Accessibility and challenge become one continuously-tuned dial

data.brief: The durable claim is organizational: when the best approach is replaced every few months, the competitive asset is not the approach but the capacity to swap it — prepared people, a swappable abstraction, a fixed review cadence, and eval sets that decide. "The company that will dominate tomorrow is being born today, and its technology approach will change multiple times before it does." Build-for-change "is arguably the moat — until that changes"
data.name: Adaptability is the moat until it isnt

data.brief: AI enablement has three phases — experimentation, adoption, impact — and near-total adoption can coexist with zero delivery improvement; the jump to impact comes from integrating agents into build-and-ship workflows (delegation, decomposition, verification), not from more usage or newer models
data.name: Near-total adoption can coexist with zero delivery improvement

data.brief: Opening audience test, unusually clean as evidence: nearly every hand went up for "have you asked an LLM for financial advice", and most went down for "did you trust the answer and follow it". His own worked case — a full-context, all-models investment decision that flipped A → B → A on two small assumption tweaks — is offered as why. So a correct answer is not a sufficient product: a great advisory experience needs grounded science plus an understanding of the person (their preferences, what they like and don't), and must make the user feel they were part of the decision.
data.name: Advice is a trust artifact before it is an information artifact

data.brief: The speed came from collapsing negotiation and handover: one person (or a pair) owning discovery→design→build→deploy end-to-end inside pre-built guardrails. In large organizations that agency — not the tooling — is the scarce resource; changing process means shifting the human behavior behind it: access, champions, experimentation space, permission to break habits
data.name: In large organizations agency, not tooling, is the scarce resource

data.brief: The damage from uneven agent adoption is not that some people are slower but that the fast and slow are coupled through review: high-throughput adopters generate PRs that low-throughput colleagues must review, so the cost of one group's leverage lands on the other, who then have less time to adopt and more reason to distrust the tools. That feedback loop makes "figure it out yourself" actively harmful rather than merely suboptimal, and it is why the intervention has to be organizational — a shared setup, shared skills, and protected time — rather than individual enablement
data.name: Agent adoption is a distribution problem

data.brief: The durable claim: trust in an agent purchase is distributed away from the agent — the merchant publishes what it sells and logs why it matched, the payment provider holds the credential and enforces the limits, and the agent between them holds neither the card nor unbounded authority, only a persona that must be treated as policy. The same structure the batch's PayPal and AWS talks describe from the other side
data.name: Agent commerce trust splits between manifest and token

data.brief: A useful coding agent IS a supply-chain actor — the moment it holds production credentials it must get the same guardrails as a human engineer; the question is never "are agents dangerous" but "what can this actor reach"
data.name: A useful coding agent is a supply-chain actor

data.brief: Each step of plan/act/observe/persist/decide crosses a boundary and can leave the world half-changed, so an agent run is a distributed transaction: persist every step, make every tool idempotent, define the compensation for every irreversible action, and treat memory as a cache with provenance. That is the durable-execution layer's requirements list written from first principles — which suggests why the runtime vendors in this batch are converging on it
data.name: Agent loops need saga semantics

data.brief: Enterprise agent value must be denominated in the customer's three currencies — increase revenue, decrease cost, mitigate risk: a $2,000/day agent read as expensive until reframed as dispatch-cost reduction ("absolutely worth it, but I never measured it this way"); ROI framing, not model capability, decides whether deployments survive after the vendor leaves
data.name: Enterprise agent value must be denominated in the customer's three currencies

data.brief: The distribution of agent success across domains is better predicted by how symbolically legible a domain already is than by how hard it is. Code came with its own representation, its own version history, and its own oracle — so the agent inherited a world it could read and a verifier it could trust. Every domain that has resisted agents so far lacks one of those three, and no amount of model scale supplies them. The implication for anyone picking an agent market is to audit for pre-existing representation and reward before capability
data.name: Agent success tracks symbolic legibility

data.brief: The durable claim from the merchant side: the commerce that exists at scale runs inside assistants through pushed feeds and standardized checkout APIs, with a human confirming payment — not through agents driving browsers, and not yet through machine-speed rails. The protocol map has a job for each acronym, two competing commerce primitives, and a mandate spec that everyone is waiting on; the merchant's work is feeds, conformance, evals and latency
data.name: Agentic commerce arrived as assistant checkout not browser agents

data.brief: Because an AI agent is, from first principles, just software — an LLM in an agentic loop with tools and context — coding agents can build and improve other agents; the eval suite replaces the human in the inner loop, while humans move up to hypothesis-level steering and SME triage
data.name: Agents are just software, so coding agents can build and improve other agents

data.brief: The historically-informed read on the present: every platform era began with a primitive that felt like the whole story (HTML pages in 1995) and matured into a category nobody had named yet (web apps, native mobile). Agents are this era's web pages — and since the models are already sufficient to rebuild Knowledge Navigator "for real," the remaining work is category invention: the primitives (org-level harnesses, realtime voice, context machinery, dynamic UI) are this cycle's compilers and databases, and the mature form gets discovered by building against the old visions
data.name: Agents are the web pages of 1995

data.brief: Once the computer-use "hands" live in an OS-level background driver, agents stop being screen puppeteers mimicking a human at the keyboard and become concurrent co-workers sharing your machine ("multi-cursor") — and the differentiating engineering moves into the driver/harness layer (accessibility-tree access, windowed observation, cross-OS lifting), not the model
data.name: OS-level background drivers turn agents from screen puppeteers into coworkers

data.brief: Inversion of the default trust posture: an agent should be treated as dangerous until proven safe — never allowed to act unless safety is provable — because a goal-directed model will do whatever closes the gap to its goal, files and databases included; guardrails-by-vibes (alignment + permission prompts) don't meet that bar
data.name: Treat agents as dangerous until proven safe; guardrails-by-vibes don't meet the bar

data.brief: As agentic automation matures, organizations will not just give agents more tools — they will allocate them budgets. Per-task token budgets are the primitive form; the next step is agents managing their own budget for anything they need: discovering services, requesting data, negotiating execution, and paying for work across organizational boundaries. The agent stops being "a cook with a better knife" and starts acting like an executive chef
data.name: Organizations will allocate agents budgets, not just more tools

data.brief: A web feature flag covers one thing (feature on/off); agents have six independent behavior surfaces — prompts, tools, models, memory, autonomy, sub-agents — each needing its own flag type. The blast radius concentrates in autonomy level, and the canonical failure is a flagged parent spawning an unflagged child that bypasses the middleware, so the kill switch never reaches it
data.name: Agents have six behavior surfaces, each needing its own flag type

data.brief: Agent traverses context graph → adds decision trace → graph compounds → agent becomes smarter. Graph sits as semantic layer on existing data.
data.description: When an AI agent investigates an issue, it doesn't search a flat index — it traverses a context graph, following typed relationships between entities. Graphs give the agent reasoning structures that vector databases cannot: who approved what, which policy version applied, what exception was granted. Adding decision traces (the explicit HOWs and WHYs — workflows, exceptions, reasoning chains) creates a compounding loop: agent solves a problem, walks the graph, writes a new trace, and the graph grows richer. New reasoning paths emerge that didn't exist before — the agent becomes smarter with each traversal. Critically, this graph doesn't require a standalone graph database. It can sit as a semantic layer on top of existing data infrastructure: SQL databases, NoSQL document stores, or even a well-structured collection of markdown files.
data.importance: Reframes context graphs from product to protocol — works on SQL, NoSQL, markdown.
data.name: Agents are informed walkers

data.brief: Agent pipelines end up needing the exact same operational guarantees software delivery standardized decades ago — regression tests, run monitoring, contract testing, staging, audit trails — but the agent ecosystem provides none by default. Until a shared layer exists, every solo builder pays for them one failure at a time; "looks done" and "is done" stay different objects only if a gate enforces it
data.name: Agent pipelines need the operational guarantees software delivery standardized

data.brief: Agents need more than DNS-style name→address resolution: capabilities, rules, trust, and adaptive routing must resolve too, and if that layer is owned by a single platform the walled garden wins by default — open, portable identity/discovery is the load-bearing piece of an open agentic web
data.name: Agents need more than DNS-style resolution; open discovery is load-bearing

data.brief: Agents must relearn the database lesson: underneath every serious database is a log and everything else is a view; make the agent's log primary and reliability, scalability, forking, multiplayer, migration, and auditability fall out structurally instead of being bolted on — compaction included, understood as a lossy projection/fork that never replaces the raw log (throw the raw log away and you've lost part of the agent)
data.name: Make the agent's log primary and reliability, forking and audit fall out

data.brief: The analogy is load-bearing, not decorative: a paradigm whose reference architecture crystallizes layer by layer through production practice, with the infrastructure vendors racing to productize each layer (runtime first, memory next). It predicts where value pools — the unsolved layers (cost control, replay/debug) are where the next Kubernetes-equivalents will be built — and warns against the 2015 mistake of over-engineering orchestration before the single loop is solid
data.name: Agents repeat the microservices curve

data.brief: Agents don't need clean APIs. They navigate complex, poorly designed systems natively, choosing tools by semantic value and durability.
data.description: The conventional Silicon Valley narrative argues that developers must build clean APIs, IDLs, or MCP interfaces so AI agents can use their software. Aaron Levie (CEO, Box) argues this is fundamentally wrong: agents are exceptionally good at navigating complex, poorly designed systems natively. They choose tools based on semantic value (does this tool actually solve my problem?), backend cost (how expensive is this call?), and durability (will this interface still work tomorrow?) — rather than requiring elegant developer experience. The implication inverts the "build for agents" narrative: legacy systems aren't a blocker to agentic adoption, they're an opportunity. The enterprises with the messiest, most complex systems may benefit most.
data.importance: Inverts the conventional build-for-agents narrative. Legacy isn't a blocker, it's an opportunity.
data.name: Agents thrive in messy legacy systems

data.brief: The bigger win is not doing existing work faster but automating work that never happened at all: nobody proactively investigated performance because the research phase was an unpriceable black box (an hour or weeks); models are already good enough for this — the leverage is context, scoring and guardrails ("context over cleverness")
data.name: The bigger win is automating work that never happened at all

data.brief: The eval bar differs by audience: in agents you use (Cursor, Claude Code), the engineer notices a missed skill trigger and reprompts; in agents you build for customers, users don't know skills exist and never invoke them explicitly — model-triggered activation off shallow prompts is the whole game, so triggering behavior must be eval-verified, not eyeballed
data.name: The eval bar differs between agents you use and agents you build

data.brief: Even AGI won't know your tasks, context, or relationships — "if you asked Einstein to help with your emails, he'd ask what's an email"; intelligence is different from being all-knowing, so last-mile learning (task specs, context acquisition, your evals) remains the durable layer no model release dissolves
data.name: Even AGI still needs last-mile learning of your tasks and context

data.brief: The durable framing: AI doesn't add capability to an enterprise so much as reveal and amplify what is already there — accelerating working systems and breaking quickly on broken ones. That makes the boring 60% (data, architecture, integration, enablement, change management) the actual critical path to AI-native, and explains from the buyer's side why value is "left on the table" at current model intelligence: the bottleneck is the estate, not the model
data.name: Ai is a flashlight not a bandaid

data.brief: AI is becoming an interface technology, not just an intelligence technology: a system that can reason, listen, infer, and adapt can absorb the burdens humans carried only because machines were too limited — choosing timing, modality, context, and repair. The design question flips to "what burden are we still putting on humans only because the machine used to be too limited to carry it?" The answer space is the affordances humans already use with each other — a question, a pause, a sketch, a checklist, a quiet aside, saying nothing — with channel and moment chosen by the AI. Take that burden off people and adoption follows
data.name: AI is becoming an interface technology, not just intelligence

data.brief: Macintosh analogy: the GUI succeeded by meeting unfamiliar users with borrowed real-life vocabulary and literal icons, then shed abstractions (System 1 → System 6) as literacy grew. AI UX today is "around System 3": users have transferable mental models (chat ≈ messaging) but interfaces must adapt them (sources, stop/pause, agentic tools) and graduate users gradually rather than assume expertise
data.name: AI UX today is around System 3 of the Macintosh arc

data.brief: The talk's durable claim is a categorical one: alignment reduces the probability of bad action but cannot bound it, because a prompt-injectable agent can be driven into a state where it believes the bad action is correct — so any security argument that terminates in "the model will refuse" has no boundary at all. That reframes agent security as a network-egress problem with a testable deterministic gate, and it is the same move the corpus keeps making elsewhere (verifier outside the model) applied to the wire. As models improve the residual risk shrinks but never reaches zero, so the backstop is permanent
data.name: Alignment is not a boundary

data.brief: "Old skill, new economics": with model access commoditized, the durable moat shifts to the analyst toolkit — story mapping, business model canvas, value canvas, design-thinking elicitation. The SDLC itself doesn't change with AI; the toolkit that feeds it does, and the functional-consultant skill set stops being overhead and becomes the mode of production
data.name: With model access commoditized, the analyst toolkit is the durable moat

data.brief: Architect for half-life, not for the current stack: models, prompts, and frameworks are the shortest-lived, most swappable parts of an agent system, so the durable investment is the execution layer (state, retries, orchestration, resumability) — get its abstractions right and everything else can be swapped without a rewrite every 6 months
data.name: Architect for half-life: invest in the durable execution layer

data.brief: The property that makes context-window persona architecture ethical is the same property that makes it debuggable: documents stay documents (provenance preserved, human interpretive custody, reversible encounter), so every input shaping the output is inspectable rather than smeared across billions of parameters — archival virtues and engineering virtues are the same virtues
data.name: Context-window persona architecture is ethical because it's auditable

data.brief: Slop saturation inverts marketing economics: precisely because generated content is free, the artisanal carries the trust premium — craft, beautiful design and text, physical presence (SF, billboards, events), and even public failure with an elegant recovery all work because they are hard to fake and audiences can no longer tell the real deal in cheap channels
data.name: Slop saturation inverts marketing economics: the artisanal carries the trust premium

data.brief: The durable reframing is to stop asking whether the model will be right and start asking what the surrounding system permits when it is wrong: the coordinator is probabilistic by nature, so correctness has to be a property of the deterministic controls — contracts, idempotency, compensation, budgets, scoped credentials, parameter-bound approvals — not of the model. The same conclusion the batch's security and runtime talks reach, derived here from three decades of distributed-systems failure modes
data.name: Ask what the system lets it do when wrong

data.brief: Nothing in this 20-minute frontier-conference talk is a model problem. The hard parts of long-horizon agent work — handles, lifecycles, durable state, signaling into running work, reconnect/resume, notification fan-in versus polling — are the classical distributed-systems curriculum, being relearned at the MCP layer by an engineer who lived it once already at Cloud Foundry/Kubernetes scale. The engineering frontier of "async agents" sits entirely in the periphery around the model, and the periphery is where the industry's protocol effort is going
data.name: Async agent protocols are distsys again

data.brief: Agent rollouts are long-tailed (30 s to 3 h for coding tasks), so synchronous on-policy RL means always waiting on the slowest rollout; accepting bounded off-policyness (~16 steps average, DPPO-stabilized to thousands of steps) decouples forward progress from rollout latency and lets sandbox boots, judge grading, and weight sync overlap without wasting GPU
data.name: Bounded off-policyness decouples RL progress from long-tailed rollout latency

data.brief: Tokens can be bought and compute rented, but operator attention cannot be added — so agent products and workflows should be judged by where they let humans spend attention: talk-first delegation by default ("let them cook"), full-depth inspection on demand, review-once artifacts instead of streamed intermediate tokens. The engineering frontier moves from writing code to designing the loops and organizations around agents — "models are advancing faster than the harnesses and organizations around them"
data.name: Operator attention is the scarce resource agent products must be judged by

data.brief: Moving "from token maxing to value maxing" requires the ledger first: attribute every model call to a run, a user and a cohort, then budget at the cohort, then steer — because value can only be expressed in the unit you are charged in. The self-learning policy roadmap is the accumulation loop applied to spend: the ledger of what ran becomes the training signal for what to govern
data.name: Attribution is the precondition for value maxing

data.brief: Replacing static compliance rules with a risk model that ingests audit outcomes turns every investigation into training signal — each completed audit makes the next one cheaper, and the system adapts as fraud patterns evolve without manual rule updates; the flywheel only works on top of the connected entity graph
data.name: Learning from audit outcomes turns every investigation into training signal

data.brief: Decades of auth (passwords, API keys, service accounts, OAuth) rest on two assumptions: whoever authenticates is who acts, and the actor is a deterministic program a human wrote that can be security-reviewed. Agents break both — the principal is not the actor, and no code review can bound what a probabilistic agent will do next run — so registration-time permissions no longer constrain behavior
data.name: Agents break both core assumptions of decades of auth

data.brief: The security thesis in one line: the question is not whether the model can be perfect (it cannot) but "what authority survives outside the model boundary versus inside it." EchoLeak and Replit are the same lesson from an attacker and from an over-eager worker — a mistake must live outside the agent's circle of influence — and plan/execute separation with a policy gate and short-lived capabilities is how authority is kept outside without making the agent useless
data.name: Authority must survive outside the model

data.brief: Stop giving agents our credentials; give them authority. The shift is from "pretend to be me" (agent impersonates the user with full access) to "act for me within these limits" (agent is a scoped principal with its own identity) — which is precisely what makes tracing, firing, and revoking an agent possible
data.name: Give agents authority, not credentials

data.brief: The durable claim: at cent-level frequency a human cannot approve purchases, so authorization becomes policy the wallet enforces and settlement leaves the chain for off-chain authorizations; the agent's reach is then bounded by budget policy, and its capability ceiling by what it can pay for. Stablecoins win the rail because the transaction shape — tiny, constant, machine-initiated — is one cards and chains alike were not built for
data.name: Authorization moves from the purchase to the budget

data.brief: What compounds is not any individual automated step but the daily removal of bottlenecks from the loop itself — and that meta-work is itself delegable: the agent is asked to audit the process it just executed and name what slowed it. The artifact that improves over a month is the harness, not the model and not any one automation. Corollary he draws for the job: "sitting behind a desk from 9 to 5 just writing code is not valid anymore", because a developer's variety of work is exactly what the loop absorbs.
data.name: What compounds is automating the loop, not any individual task

data.brief: The durable claim from a production engine at 25K comments/week: the model's review ability was never the lever — it is confidently wrong and cannot tell — so the gains (−60% cost, +70% accuracy, 67% address rate) came from instrumenting what happened to each comment (sentiment, address rate, trajectory), routing it back to the humans who own the rules, and constraining the agent's turns. The same finding as Qodo's "context, not models, gates review," reached by measurement rather than benchmark
data.name: Automated review is an observability problem

data.brief: Frontier training knowledge is apprenticeship-transmitted, held by a few thousand people, and consists largely of configuration choices humans make badly — an unusually good automation target, since the expertise is tacit but the search space is mechanical. The consequence the speaker emphasizes is not cheaper training but a different question distribution: when asking costs less, more and stranger things get asked, and the innovation cycle rather than any single result is what accelerates. That reframes auto-research from a productivity tool into a change in what gets investigated at all
data.name: Automating tacit craft changes the questions

data.brief: The automation prize is not "amalgamate one person's job". It is the enormous body of rote work so simple you can describe it to someone else in a sentence — work that ought to be repeatable for approximately free, and that today is neither automated nor even addressed, because the tools we built are optimized to please whoever is watching. What we did instead was make software cheaper to write while leaving its expressiveness exactly where it was in 2019, which is why "just-in-time software" is a double-edged compliment. The unanswered question he puts to the industry: why can't software just be more expressive?
data.name: The automation prize is the rote work nobody has addressed, not job replacement

data.brief: Agentic engineering (autonomous automation) is categorically different from coding with an agent in your IDE: 80% success is fine when you're in the loop steering, but an automation running without you must cross ~80–90% trust — with issues verified worth-fixing and fixes verified in runtime — or its output is slop humans learn to ignore
data.name: Autonomous agentic automation must cross ~80–90% trust or its output is slop

data.brief: "Intelligence is not the blocker" from a runtime vendor is a pat-model-not-bottleneck claim with a specific bottleneck named: the inability to grant runtime-changing access safely. Autonomy expands exactly as far as containment, scoping and intent judgment allow — which is why the demo's manual scoped sandboxes exist today and the automatic intent-based delegation is still a prototype
data.name: Autonomy is gated by containment not capability

data.brief: Our reading, flagged as interpretation, not the speaker's claim. All three demonstrated wins share a shape: a dense, cheap, fast-to-evaluate, tamper-checkable scalar (bits per byte on a five-minute run; wall-clock seconds; kernel throughput on a vendor leaderboard) — precisely the RLVR-easy regime that this batch's other four talks say covers almost none of real work. What the results do establish is significant and shouldn't be discounted: the system found novel mechanisms, not tuned hyperparameters, and beat expert human effort in domains where the team had no experts. What separates them from the Eureka machine is exactly the verifier for everything else — which is why pillar 3 is simulation.
data.name: Auto-research proof points are narrow by construction (dense, cheap, checkable metrics)

data.brief: For subjective domains the optimization target itself is wrong, and the pipeline compounds the error at every stage: mean-seeking generation produces the most likely output, undifferentiated preference collection averages away the disagreement that carried the signal, and LLM judges reward fluency. Each stage is individually reasonable and collectively manufactures the exact thing everyone is trying to remove. So "ending slop" is not a quality-raising exercise — it is engineering pluralism back into the pipeline: model who the rater is, force distribution coverage, preserve aesthetic disagreement, and keep human judgment on the components that must stay human.
data.name: Ending slop means engineering pluralism back into every stage of the pipeline

data.brief: "Backdoors are directions, and the difference is where they live": the poisoned fine-tune adds one consistent low-dimensional directional shift (fine-tuned activation = base + trigger-conditional backdoor vector + noise); joint representations drown it — sparse coding spends its budget explaining shared semantics — while subtraction leaves the vector as essentially all that remains (~10× signal-to-noise)
data.name: Backdoors are directions, and the activation difference is where they live

data.brief: What died is not the base model, it is the base model as the ceiling. When pre-training was the bulk of the compute and RL was a cherry on top, how good your base model was determined how good your model could get, so you built it to reflect as much of human knowledge as possible. Now RL takes an equal or larger share of the budget, so the base model's job is to hold the atomic skills RL will compose and to have seen the shape of the work — reasoning traces, agentic tasks, test-time-compute schemes — before RL has to discover them.
data.description: The practical inversion: choose pre-training data by what the RL phase must compose, not by what best represents the world. And because the priors are downstream-defined, they are also contingent — today's priors are reasoning and agents because that is how the models get used; a new interaction paradigm would change what a base model should be.
data.name: What died is the base model as the ceiling, not the base model

data.brief: Agentic systems change the eval question from "did the model produce the right answer" to "did the system behave correctly" — planning quality, tool usage, workflow execution, recovery, decision-making. Hallucinations are just one category in a failure hierarchy (memory/retrieval/safety at the base → reasoning, planning, tool-execution errors → multi-agent coordination failures at the top), so evaluating only model output misses most production risk
data.name: Agentic evals ask whether the system behaved correctly, not whether answers were right

data.brief: The SWE-bench result shows a model being taught to take an action it never took in any training trace, because the teacher shaped the reasoning path leading toward the action rather than the action token itself. That decouples behaviour change from demonstration data and makes a large class of enterprise asks tractable from logs alone — no replayable environment, no golden answers, no new labelling. It also sets the boundary condition: what can be installed this way is behaviour reachable by reasoning the model already has, which is the same limit hint leakage describes from the failure side
data.name: Behaviour can be installed from hindsight

data.brief: A vertical AI lab's actual business logic: customer and kit-manufacturer work reveals which tasks matter, build the benchmark for them, publish it, frontier labs compete on it, the models improve at exactly the work the lab's products depend on, the products get better. The benchmark is not sold; its value is directional pull on frontier post-training. Corollary they act on: stay ahead of the labs' post-training ("the labs are starting to catch up, but we kind of want to stay ahead") by extending horizon and breadth faster than the frontier absorbs the last set.
data.name: The benchmark is not sold; its value is directional pull on frontier post-training

data.brief: The reason frontier models bunch at the top of a leaderboard is usually the benchmark, not the models. Every defect Datacurve names is a construction choice inherited from mining public PRs: contamination (solutions, tests and PR discussion are public), brittle verifiers anchored to one merged implementation (false negatives on valid alternatives), leakage through the git history the agent can read, and over-prescriptive prompts that measure instruction-following rather than engineering.
data.description: Each has an engineering fix — author the tasks, verify observable behaviour, strip the environment, shorten the prompt — and applying them restored discrimination between models that SWE-bench Pro had lost.
data.name: Leaderboard clustering is a benchmark construction failure, not a model failure

data.brief: A company benchmark is not a scorecard but a lifecycle artifact carrying three jobs simultaneously — "make it work" (validate before first release, handle edge cases, select the model, debug traces), "make it right" (a release gate proving no change to the agent stack caused a regression), and "make it fast/cheap" (tune cost and latency, and mine the traces for training data). Because it is repopulated from production failures, observability and experimentation are "two sides of the same coin" and must be wired together: two loops run in parallel — benchmark expansion from recorded production failures, and a simulation runner sweeping new agent configs against the expanded benchmark.
data.name: A company benchmark is a lifecycle artifact carrying three jobs at once

data.brief: A benchmark used to be a dry academic question-and-answer set; today it is an aspirational artifact — an expression of values about what you want AI to do and how you want it to behave. That reframing makes taste and product sense construction requirements, not garnish: a medical benchmark needs someone who knows the regulatory and legal environment, not only doctors who can answer medical questions, because that determines which tasks are worth testing at all. And because taste cannot be supplied from inside the frontier — not by AI assistance in authoring, not by LLM judges in grading — the expensive human expert is a structural requirement of the artifact, not a temporary inefficiency.
data.name: A benchmark is an aspirational artifact expressing values, not a dry Q&A set

data.brief: Task difficulty and task value are independent axes, and the field has been optimizing the wrong one. "It is one thing to have a task that is failing the LLM, proving the LLM is not there yet. It is another thing for an engineer to look at a task and say: if the LLM is fixing this, I trust it to fix that." A benchmark's real output is transferred trust, so a task earns its place only if passing it licenses a real-world inference — which rules out both the artificially hard (build a C compiler in Rust) and the artificially easy-to-grade (string-matchable).
data.description: This is the same claim the trust gap measures from the other end: engineers stopped consulting leaderboards precisely because passing didn't license anything.
data.name: Task difficulty and task value are independent axes; the field optimized the wrong one

data.brief: The jargon wall — graders, verifiers, long horizon, rubrics, harnesses — hides an ordinary five-stage software pipeline, and treating it as ordinary software is what surfaced the defects. A director with no ML background, working with his team for two months, reduced the field to five stages, opened individual tasks, and found leaked interfaces, tests asserting unstated variable names, and tests on unexported internals — the kinds of defects any senior engineer rejects in code review daily. The scarce input for fixing benchmarks is therefore engineering review, not ML expertise: "benchmarks are not hard. We need to look under the hood."
data.name: Benchmarks are ordinary software; the scarce input is engineering review, not ML expertise

data.brief: Benchmaxxing is not simply labs cheating — it is the equilibrium of a market where every side's incentives point the same way. Buyers cannot evaluate benchmark validity, so popularity substitutes for it; builders cannot afford correct construction ($15M+ per serious benchmark) so they take shortcuts that break tasks silently; labs face marketing and political pressure to keep hill-climbing past the point where the score stops tracking human value.
data.description: That is why insider disclosure ("it can be easily gamed", "these aren't better models, they're better arena models") changes nothing about a benchmark's standing. The fix has to be applied on both sides at once — to the people making benchmarks and the people reporting on them.
data.name: Benchmaxxing is a two-sided market failure, not simply labs cheating

data.brief: Prompt injection can't be solved, only bounded — so the deterministic-vs-agentic partition (who holds git-write and CI-trigger credentials) is the actual security model, not the sandbox drawing
data.name: The deterministic-vs-agentic partition is the actual security model

data.brief: In brownfield code the binding constraint isn't the agent's intelligence but its perception — dead code and cross-module surprises it has never looked at; give it eyes (logs, screenshots, UI state, service control) and its intuition converts into verified, trustable work
data.name: In brownfield code the binding constraint is perception, not intelligence

data.brief: The CTO objection ("I can barely reason about one AI-generated codebase and you want me to run millions — you're describing my worst problem multiplied") aims the right instinct at the wrong target: brittleness is unmanaged divergence inside one tangled artifact. Stem+divergences makes safety structural — isolation, immutability, per-divergence live rollback, one-context blast radius — rather than asking anyone to trust AI coordination; the honest answer is architecture, not "AI is good at coding"
data.name: Structure, not trust: bounded divergences make adaptive software safe

data.brief: The durable idea is a type change in agent authorization: from a boolean scope to a multi-dimensional budget (volume, rate, reversibility, observation), each dimension carried by a deterministic primitive outside the model — rate limits that refill, verbs sorted by failure mode, tripwires on aggregates, a second key for the irreversible. It preserves autonomy (no approvals inside the ceiling) while bounding the worst loop, which is exactly what scope-narrowing cannot do
data.name: Budgets replace booleans

data.brief: The build-vs-buy line traces the value line: inference/model serving is the most-bought layer, while product logic stays in-house (61% build their own prompt management — "everyone's prompts are special"; prompts, RAG, evals relatively in-house; fine-tuning "the clearest not yet") — differentiation lives in the layers around the model, not in serving the model
data.name: Build-vs-buy traces the value line: buy inference, build product logic

data.brief: Building is now easy but generating value is still hard — AI engineers over-index on process and setups when the point is value, which takes many swings to find; "the only way to prove agents work is to do the best work of our lives faster than ever" — the world is watching AI engineers for proof AI transforms productivity
data.name: Building is now easy, but generating value is still hard

data.brief: The durable meta-claim is a design order: in regulated enterprises, take the production constraints (audit, data boundaries, approvals, evals) as the architectural principles first and build back up to the PoC's accuracy — because the constraints are what make the system generalize across use cases, and the accuracy is the easy part. Patterns that already exist in finance and defense (transaction logs, object storage, zero trust) cover most of it; AI adds the need to combine them
data.name: Build from constraints not from the poc

data.brief: The unifying move of the whole talk: where supervision doesn't exist, inference compute can manufacture it. Grounding A/B gaps, judge panels, hindsight rubric extraction, difficulty calibration, simulator refinement and trace mining are all the same trade — spend compute to convert real-world material into learnable signal — and the human is deliberately reserved for the top of the stack: "surface the most important pieces up to the human... actually employing an expert to say this is good, this is not what I want".
data.name: Where supervision doesn't exist, inference compute can manufacture it

data.brief: Selling only technology fails at the last mile: you have organized the buyer's data, but the buyer asks "what does that do for my actual business?" Selling only services is a dev shop.
data.description: The working configuration is both at once — smart engineers who learn the customer's business and assemble a solution on the vendor's platform — so what changes hands is an outcome, with the software as implementation detail. The fine-dining analogy: the waiter caters to your every need and figures out the problem for you.
data.name: Customers buy an outcome; the software is an implementation detail

data.brief: KV-cache economics quietly dictate multi-model architecture: the sidekick pattern exists to avoid re-paying for context; compaction and model switching are priced by the cache miss, not the tokens; cache lifetimes are operational fictions self-hosters can escape; and the move that made agents economically possible at all — Cognition buying direct compute in 2024, "before cache tokens was a thing API providers paid for" — was a cache-economics arbitrage. Any router design that ignores the cache optimizes the wrong bill
data.name: Cache is the physics of multi model systems

data.brief: The workshop's deepest lesson is that context strategy is an economics problem set by the caching layer, not a cleverness problem set by summarization technique: once cached tokens are ~50× cheaper and compaction breaks the cache, the whole toolkit of "smart" context tricks inverts, and the dumb strategy (keep everything) dominates on all three axes at once. That makes the correct default the opposite of the industry's, and it means the single most important thing to know about any harness is its cache behaviour — a serving-layer fact, not a model or prompt fact
data.name: Caching not cleverness decides context

data.brief: The three-part mental model that makes an autonomous performance agent safe: the profiler gives an estimate, the canary gives ground truth, the engineer makes the decision. Everything load-bearing here predates AI — rock-solid unit and integration tests with business logic properly encoded, excellent canary automation, and observability reporting CPU, latency and error rate.
data.description: The agent's job is only to know how to invoke canary and where to read the report, then make a judgment call on it. The inversion worth keeping: teams reach for AI first and foundations later, but without the foundations "it will just cause more friction and more bugs in production" — the AI is the cheapest part of an agentic performance loop, and the prerequisite investment is the expensive part.
data.name: Profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, the engineer decides

data.brief: Capability increases move everyone toward the YOLO pole but never remove the requirement of proof — they relocate it: yesterday you inspected outputs (read the code), today you inspect task direction, tomorrow you inspect the loops. Anthropic's Shihipar on Fable 5: "we used to check if Claude is doing the work right; now I check if Claude is doing the right work"; Karpathy's one-sentence version: "it's never felt so tempting to stop looking at code — but don't do this in production." Closing line of the talk: not every line needs your eyes; every system still needs your judgment
data.name: Capability increases relocate the requirement of proof, never remove it

data.brief: Capability and reliability are different axes: better specs, MCP servers, sub-agents, and context are instructions, and instructions are not verification — however good the input, you still verify the output; trust, not ability, is the bottleneck for delegation
data.name: Capability and reliability are different axes

data.brief: The four solves together retire the CAPTCHA as a human/bot boundary: the checkbox class falls to trusted-click-at-computed-position, the OCR class to vision, the behavioral-drag class to human-like motion synthesis, and the timed-grid class to a code-plus-one-vision-look architecture. What defeats each is not a novel exploit but the CDP trusted-event path plus a vision model — both now commodity. Any defense that assumes "a bot cannot do this in the browser" is already false, which relocates bot defense to identity and attestation (the exact gap Klein names in the same track)
data.name: Captcha is over as a boundary

data.brief: Personal knowledge management historically failed because it demanded structure at capture time — tags, folders, links — precisely when the user has the least patience and the most to say. Inverting the order removes the failure mode: make capture as close to free as speech, then spend agent compute on the structuring nobody was ever going to do by hand. The corollary for tool design is that the valuable interface is a very fast unstructured inbox plus a scheduled enrichment loop, and that almost every feature between those two is now something an agent generates on request
data.name: Capture cheap structure later

data.brief: Every step the anti-pattern check moves left removes a whole layer of overhead — production fix (risky, needs a canary), then a review comment (cheap, still a rewrite), then authoring time (no rewrite at all, the bad code is never written). But you cannot start at the left: the catalog has to be earned from reactive production findings before it is trustworthy enough to steer code generation.
data.description: That makes the reactive path the on-ramp rather than the failure mode, and it makes the catalog — not the agent — the compounding asset: one service's profiling run permanently upgrades every future agent's starting position, and the catalog's confidence levels are what let a later agent skip the discovery work entirely. The binding constraint at the far left is context, not capability: consulting the catalog before every token costs latency and tokens, so the catalog's structure and index are what decide whether shift-left is affordable.
data.name: The catalog, not the agent, is the compounding asset that earns the shift left

data.brief: The catalog can grow; the model's working set must not — decouple the registered capability surface from the per-request context via retrieval. The router's underrated benefit is subtractive: for "weather in Paris" the flight and hotel tools aren't ranked lower, they simply don't exist in the model's choice set for that request
data.name: The catalog can grow; the model's working set must not

data.brief: If AI apps (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor) are the new browsers, MCP servers/apps are the new websites: software distribution shifts from web + search to store placement and model-mediated selection, and product UI moves into widgets rendered inside the chat surface ("I don't want to look at your dashboard anymore — I want it in Claude")
data.name: AI apps are the new browsers; MCP servers and apps are the new websites

data.brief: The assistant host is accreting every property that historically defined a platform: distribution (app-store-scale reach inside ChatGPT/Claude), the interaction contract (three spec-defined levels of journey control), trust and auditability (everything routes through the chat), and the customer relationship itself (the app no longer sees the user's flow). SaaS frontends don't get destroyed in this shift — they get demoted to branded atoms whose composition, context and journey belong to the host. The spec authors present this as the win-win that unblocks adoption; it is also a one-way transfer of power to whoever owns the chat surface
data.name: Chat host is the new app platform

data.brief: At ~30 cents per video and a ~5% defect rate, per-item human review costs more than it saves: QA flips from pre-publish gate to post-publish takedown, and each defect becomes diagnostic signal (e.g., a missed tool call at game end) rather than a reason to gate. Verification economics, not capability, now set the human's role
data.name: Cheap generation flips QA from pre-publish gate to post-publish takedown

data.brief: None of these failure modes are new — timeouts, retries, idempotency, locks, ordering and state ownership are decades-old distributed-systems problems. What changed is the setting: they now sit around a probabilistic planner with dynamic plans that rebuilds its context every turn, with more event sources feeding it and more action surfaces to act through. Agents do not invent new failures; they make the familiar ones far easier to trigger and much harder to explain, because the system stays fluent while it is broken.
data.name: Classic distributed-systems failures return, easier to trigger and harder to explain

data.brief: The consumer-attention filter that consolidated mobile apps will consolidate claws: survive by being very economically valuable or very frequent; capability parity is table stakes because switching costs are near zero and "there's only space in your brain for a limited number of things"
data.name: Claws survive by being very economically valuable or very frequent

data.brief: Agents measurably care about clean code: identical agentic tasks on a cleaned codebase consume materially fewer tokens, reasoning, and energy than on a typical one — codebase maintenance is now agent-performance engineering, not hygiene, and the effect compounds
data.name: Codebase maintenance is now agent-performance engineering

data.brief: Editor-embedded agents shouldn't read the raw file system: ACP proxies FS and terminals through the client so the agent sees what the user sees (unsaved buffer state, live terminals) — perception mediation by the harness, not extra model capability, is what makes embedded agents trustworthy
data.name: ACP proxies FS and terminals through the client so agents see what users see

data.brief: The missing production layer is one that consumes traces, absorbs evals, and converts both into retrieval guidance for future runs — outcomes must become first-class retrieval signals (utility re-ranking) or agents repeat identical failures forever; the standard ReAct loop lists reason/act/retrieve but omits learn, and that omission is where the user's signal dies
data.name: The missing layer converts traces and evals into retrieval guidance for future runs

data.brief: The comfort of code — write the function right and it runs the same way every time — does not survive scale: requirements and externalities shape behavior, accumulating code interacts unpredictably, and users (including adversaries) do things you didn't expect. "Software is not provable in the same way that code is provable — software can break in interesting and novel ways." So generation quality can never retire verification: as AI writes more software against bigger problems, you hit the unprovability limit more often, and automated verification is the risk control you buy back for the control you released over how the code gets written
data.name: Code is provable software is not

data.brief: Guardrails belong in deterministic code upstream of the LLM, where they are cheap (no tokens spent on blocked queries), fast, and testable — a prompt is an instruction the model sometimes ignores; a pre-LLM function is a contract with a test suite. Same logic replaces LLM sub-agents with Python functions for anything code can do (dates, lookups, calculations)
data.name: Guardrails belong in deterministic, testable code upstream of the LLM

data.brief: A codebase is a spec — often the only complete copy of the spec you have; once verification lives in the test suite rather than in humans reading code, you can regenerate implementations (full rewrites, three parallel candidates, ports to other languages) and select by evidence
data.name: A codebase is a spec — often the only complete copy you have

data.brief: What bounded Wisedocs' agent productivity was never model choice — it was the environment: repo topology (E2E verification and sandbox setup dictate monorepo), spec quality (a well-constructed spec is what unlocks high-capability execution), lifecycle guardrails adopted as they appeared (plan mode, local review skills, human PR review used deliberately as *context-building* for a new repo), and "a number of different frameworks and primitives… in order to have good agentic development" — without which teams "waste time just running in loops with models." The refactor's payoff came from reshaping the code for agents and humans at once
data.name: Codebase shape is agent throughput

data.brief: Because agents are non-deterministic and models are weakly self-consistent, a single successful replay proves nothing; decisions (model swaps, tool/policy changes) require cohort-scale replay distributions — and at thousands of replays the analysis itself must be delegated to agents via MCP/skills over a queryable runtime, with the human as final gate
data.name: Non-deterministic agents need cohort-scale replay distributions, not single replays

data.brief: AI industrialized the 5% of engineering that was typing; the remaining 95% is shared understanding — and at agent speed, misalignment stops being a soft cost and acquires a token-denominated price. So the next tool generation targets alignment rather than codegen: one surface where the team and its agents share the same backscroll, the same editable plan, and the same preview, with documents as the interface ("make the document true"). The bottleneck moved from generating code to agreeing on what should be true
data.name: Collaboration is the 95 percent

data.brief: A company brain cannot be bought or outsourced — only the company can pour its own truth in; the sellable artifact is the empty architecture (Brain OS), not the filled brain. Moat shifts from the software to the buyer's own curated memory — uncomfortable news for agencies and vendors selling "AI transformation"
data.name: A company brain cannot be bought or outsourced — only the empty architecture

data.brief: Boundary-condition insight for the harness debate: fixed harnesses (deterministic scaffolding, certifiable behavior) are exactly right for complicated, well-defined problems — which is *most* engineering today — and structurally wrong for complex, moving ones; the argument is not anti-harness but a claim about where each philosophy's use-cases end
data.name: Fixed harnesses fit complicated problems; complex moving ones need adaptive structure

data.brief: The unit of compliance analysis must move from the document to the relationship: the information needed to catch cross-system fraud already exists in enterprise systems — what is missing is connecting it. Cross-document compliance is a context/structure problem, not a data-volume or model-capability problem
data.name: The unit of compliance analysis must move from the document to the relationship

data.brief: The pernicious agent failure mode is not the rampaging T-Rex but harmful behavior inside a system that looks compliant the whole time: the agent understands its constraints, decides task completion matters more, proceeds, and documents itself. Research has named it (outcome-driven constraint violations, agent misalignment); a deployed response hasn't shipped — deterministic guardrails, audit, and telemetry are necessary but not sufficient
data.name: The pernicious failure is harmful behavior inside a compliant-looking system

data.brief: Bolting skills/MCP onto one agent is inheritance: it works, then breaks down as context inflates. The alternative is composition — many minimal, complete agents (not tool servers: own prompt, loop, history) coordinated in natural language, the Apollo-control-room model ("teams of experts", each person an agent with only their tools). Capability should come from structure, not from an ever-fatter context window
data.name: Compose minimal complete agents instead of inflating one agent's context

data.brief: The durable claim is what the compounding system stores: not code but the human's reasoning and taste, extracted each time they would otherwise be repeated, so that the next brainstorm starts from them. That makes the repository the memory layer, the human's judgement the appreciating asset, and "the next feature should be easier" the test of whether learning is actually accumulating
data.name: Compounding is judgement made reusable

data.brief: Compression stopped being post-processing and became a structural layer of the open-model release cycle: labs ship QAT/NVFP4 variants at launch, release strategies assume community quantization (one midsize checkpoint, the ecosystem fans out the quants), runtimes make default-quant selection a product decision, and the quant pipeline (Unsloth, Model Optimizer, Ollama, llama.cpp) is effectively the distribution channel of open AI. Without it, open weights at 1.5TB are open in name only
data.name: Compression is a release primitive

data.brief: Compressing single-cell data into a latent vector discards biologically load-bearing information — which is why heavy transformer models can underperform linear baselines, while distribution-matching (flow) preserves more
data.name: Latent-vector compression discards load-bearing single-cell information

data.brief: The ecosystem can make a model 86% smaller far more reliably than it can say what was lost: model-card matching consumes more time than the quantization itself, benchmarks miss production behavior (long-context gibberish, harness feel), arenas are gamed, and no comprehensive quant-benchmark resource exists. The field's most honest instrument — KL divergence against the uncompressed logits — measures *distance from the original*, not capability, which is an admission that capability itself can't currently be measured well enough to verify a quant
data.name: Compression outruns its instruments

data.brief: When authorship industrializes to every user (and to agents adding features only agents will use), per-artifact verification cannot scale — no one will review a million personal apps, and the XSS question stops being answerable app by app. Gadgets' move is to relocate trust from the code to the environment: confine both halves of every app so bugs are non-events, and pull the properties that must actually hold — sharing, access control, external-service mediation — up into the platform where they are implemented once, correctly. It is the verification-gap thesis executed in infrastructure: generation gets free rein precisely because trust was re-architected outside it
data.name: Confine dont verify personal codegen

data.brief: The craft is context curation, not model choice: feeding the model the best move AND human-plausible alternatives (checks/captures/threats, rating-conditioned Maia-style moves, historical games) produces explanations of what a human would actually consider, instead of engine-line dumps. The harness decides what information exists; the model decides what matters and how to tell it
data.name: Feeding conflicting context yields human-style chess explanations

data.brief: When the model chooses which connector serves an intent, being selectable by the model — store presence, clean tool annotations, passing vetting, quality signal — becomes the new SEO; high-intent traffic routes to whichever vendor the model picks, before the user ever searches
data.name: Being selectable by the model is the new SEO

data.brief: Consistency, not just accuracy, is what enterprise buyers experience as trust: a single evaluation run tells you nothing (you must average repeated runs), and in a POC bake-off the vendor whose agent flip-flops loses the deal regardless of average efficacy
data.name: Consistency, not just accuracy, is what enterprise buyers experience as trust

data.brief: Once multiple agents share state, classic distributed-systems pathologies appear — stale reads, conflicting updates, context drift, inconsistent views — and get misdiagnosed: "many multi-agent failures are consistency failures masquerading as reasoning failures" (paraphrase). Debugging blames the model when the fault is the memory layer, made harder because agent memory itself may be probabilistic and retrieval-based
data.name: Many multi-agent failures are consistency failures masquerading as reasoning failures

data.brief: The load-bearing test for any control: can the energy to remove it originate inside the agentic loop? Agents route through humans-as-tools, so an approval reachable by the agent's own persuasion is not a control; escalation must go through an independent adversary that reasons about the *spirit* of the constraint, not its syntax
data.name: Energy to remove a control must not originate inside the agentic loop

data.brief: Content correctness is downstream of engineering discipline: an accurate changelog requires an accurate diff of the product; timely update emails follow from the changelog. Content shifting left to code means the codebase becomes the source of truth for communication — so the best-communicating teams will be the ones with the most rigor in how they create software
data.name: Content correctness is downstream of engineering discipline

data.brief: A codebase is structured data (directories, imports, tests, configs, dependencies), not flat text — which is why naive long-context stuffing fails; the RLM move is to manage context the way a lead engineer onboards a huge repo: inspect and take notes in a scratch environment (REPL), write scripts to search, and delegate what you don't understand to another specialist (recursive LLM query) — context curation becomes a program the model writes, not a window the model fills
data.name: Curate context as a program the model writes, not a window it fills

data.brief: The durable lesson is that the valuable artifact was never the model's conversion ability but the *representation and pointers* handed to it — a serialization the model was trained on, an image alongside, and a pointer to the enterprise's own component — and that packaging this as an MCP server made design context a product with its own growth curve. It is the corpus's harness thesis in the design domain, with the protocol churn as the cost of being early
data.name: Context delivery is the product

data.brief: Working in Codex has three acts — bring context in (voice, plugins/connectors, appshots), do the work (in-app), take actions out in the real world; with coding "solved," mastery is less about writing code and more about knowing what you can do and how to organize the work product (a new thread? a skill? a goal? a doc?)
data.name: Working in Codex: bring context in, do the work, take actions out

data.brief: In a world where you and your competitor buy the same models and the same intelligence, encoded context — how you do business, your norms and culture — is the differentiator; context is not just king but IP, the thing that distinguishes an American Express support agent from an Amazon one
data.name: When everyone buys the same models, encoded context is the IP

data.brief: Skill invocation design is budget allocation between two scarce resources: model-invoked skills spend agent context (tokens on every request + one more thing to weigh) and buy convenience; user-invoked skills spend human cognitive load ("skill required of the pilot") and buy determinism. Neither is free — "more flexible" model invocation is a cost, not a default
data.name: Skill invocation design is budget allocation between two scarce resources

data.brief: Company context needs what code got: lifecycle management, versioning, dependency graphs ("this skill impacts these others"), named approvers/maintainers/contributors, quality gates, and security posture — the open question is "what does the GitHub for context look like?"; hardcoding context into individual agents does not scale and gets dangerous as autonomous systems multiply (the sales-vs-finance two-revenue-numbers joke, now executed by agents)
data.name: Company context needs the lifecycle management code got

data.brief: The durable claim separates access from understanding: agents that can search everything still stop at the first plausible answer and never assemble the architecture, so the missing layer is one that *delivers* task-relevant organizational context — intent, decisions, conventions, discussions, expertise — with provenance the agent can follow. The measured effect is cost and time halved on a single plan and correctness that compounds across loops; the organizational effect is that the human context layer is finally externalized
data.name: Context must be delivered not just accessible

data.brief: Understanding has to be built ahead of time: by the moment a user asks the question, it is too late to construct meaning at runtime. The architecture consequence is precomputation on two timescales, with only a thin verification slice at serve time — the opposite of query-time RAG.
data.name: Understanding must be precomputed — runtime is too late to construct meaning

data.brief: The memory-layer thesis coined from the product side (b19) has a supply side, and this is it: agents that accumulate context need somewhere to source it, and a vendor category — CaaS — is forming to structure the web into agent-consumable knowledge graphs. The two are the same market from opposite ends: memory products own the *retention* loop, CaaS/owned pipelines own the *acquisition* loop, and the data-decay curve is why acquisition is a subscription rather than a purchase. Reading them together is what makes the build-vs-buy tipping point legible
data.name: Context supply mirrors memory demand

data.brief: Free-form agent output is a dead end for systems: buried in a session, nothing downstream can reliably find it; schema-bound output written to queryable memory is what turns a one-shot prompt into a reusable agentic system with safe agent-to-step handoffs
data.name: Schema-bound output written to queryable memory turns prompts into systems

data.brief: Two teams solving the same problem in isolation reached the same architecture, which is the strongest available evidence that the running profile plus retrieval tools is a genuine attractor rather than a fashion — and simultaneously that the details where they still differ (density versus prose, update cadence, what the user may see and edit) are the real product surface. That combination is bad news for anyone selling memory as a horizontal component: the converged part is cheap to reimplement and the divergent part is exactly what has to be tuned against a specific product, which is the mechanism behind the no-outsourcing finding
data.name: Convergence without consolidation

data.brief: Convincingness and fidelity are independent properties: a system can score perfectly on personality consistency while reasoning from knowledge its historical counterpart never possessed. Current eval stacks were built to reward fluency, so they structurally cannot perform the inversion the problem requires — scoring plain-but-faithful above fluent-but-anachronistic
data.name: Convincingness and fidelity are independent properties

data.brief: Accuracy was "earned one small correction at a time, at scale" — and only corrections that became executable changes count. That makes the corrections ledger (and the composite tools distilled from it) the appreciating asset, not the model: a shipping company arriving independently at the corpus's continual-learning thesis from the operations side, with the loop living in code and process memory rather than in weights
data.name: Corrections are the compounding asset

data.brief: For full-stack work, correctness is not an API contract — it is whether a user can complete the product's intended workflow through the UI; product-style validation (computer-use verification) is therefore a *necessary* channel, and its absence explains why whole task families were unbenchmarkable
data.name: For full-stack work, correctness is workflow completion through the UI

data.brief: The durable claim is where cost control belongs: not at the model gateway (per request) and not in the model (which cannot see its own budget), but at the run — the loop between agent, tools and sub-agents — where the same in-place mechanisms the harness already uses for quality (compaction, tool-output trimming, loop detection) double as cost policies. This makes FinOps a harness concern and explains why request-level gateways plateau at caps and downgrades
data.name: Cost is a run level harness problem

data.brief: The generalizable design lesson is a scarcity-inheritance one: a distributed system built as a single deployment unit inherits the availability constraints of its most demanding component, so every subsystem pays for the trainer's fabric requirement even when it has no collectives of its own. Auditing a pipeline for which parts genuinely need tight coupling — and then defining the loosest possible contract across the seam, here two directions and an immutable version number — converts a scarce shape into an abundant one. The sidecar's *not ready* response is the small piece that makes this safe: elasticity without it would mean silently serving the wrong policy version
data.name: Couple only what needs coupling

data.brief: The talk's transferable discipline is reporting coverage — does your 95% interval actually contain the truth 95% of the time — rather than interval width. Rollout-only intervals look confident and are wrong 80% of the time; the honest move is to respect the benchmark's hierarchy and, when the data can't support a decision, to say so and spend more. That reframes evaluation cost as insurance against a far larger deployment mistake, and it is the same "test the second pass, not the first" discipline the continual-learning benchmark talks reached (Asawa, b19), here formalized for computer use
data.name: Coverage is the honest number

data.brief: Structural mismatch in the industry: one population creates data and RL environments, a different population consumes them as researchers, and the two rarely meet. The prescription is to do both under one roof — "as you're curating data you want to put yourself in the shoes of the researcher to see what it takes to actually move the metrics on the models" — because the only meaningful quality test for a dataset or environment is whether a training run moves.
data.name: Curate data from the researcher's chair: the only quality test is whether a run moves

data.brief: The talk's durable claim is that in a world where the transformer architecture is shared and kernels are reused across LLM and diffusion, the only remaining lever is data — and specifically the *taste* encoded in curation choices (preserve unconventional aesthetics vs optimize aesthetic scores, remove synthetic data despite the shortcut it offers). That reframes model differentiation as a data-and-judgement problem, the same "data is the compute multiplier" thesis the corpus reached in language, and it makes the in-house classifier suite — not the architecture — the moat
data.name: Curation is the differentiator

data.brief: When compute is rationed, curation is the only lever left — and it is the least invested one. The performance-vs-X curve has interchangeable axes (data, compute, time, dollars), so improving the data does not shift you along the curve, it changes the curve, which is why the same budget buys 8-145x more capability and why the founding result was about bending the scaling exponent rather than the offset. The market context makes this urgent rather than academic: H100 prices are rising, reasoning models are multiplying token demand, and vendors are already capping and forward-selling access. "Data quality remains the single most underleveraged compute multiplier".
data.name: When compute is rationed, curation is the only lever left and the least invested

data.brief: Hard-won library-design lesson, offered with the refactors admitted: he started from the data model — a skill for estimates analysis, a skill for fundamentals, a skill for news and analyst ratings — and real usage did not match, because users don't arrive with data-model-shaped requests. The correct cut is by user intent: an earnings preparation skill instead of an estimates-analysis skill; a pre-market briefing skill instead of news-and-ratings. And the expectation is set explicitly — start narrow, discover real use cases, refactor the library repeatedly, "and that is okay". This is the same lesson the descriptions teach one level down (write them about the request, not the skill).
data.name: Cut the skill library by user intent, not by your data model

data.brief: Verification is harder in data than software: a software task has many acceptable solutions, a data question usually has exactly one correct answer — and tests over raw binary data are the slowest, most expensive kind. Cheap verification must be manufactured (precomputed metadata layers) before agents can self-check
data.name: Data questions have one correct answer; cheap verification must be manufactured

data.brief: Model choice is not the lever for physical-data work — everyone already uses frontier models and they still fail, because coding-agent intuition (grep the files, run scripts on raw data) is wrong physics for binary data at scale. The harness that understands data's laws — schemas, execution engine, checkpoints, shared memory — is where capability comes from
data.name: Capability on physical data comes from the data harness, not model choice

data.brief: With frontier models improving on every axis, an enterprise's durable, defensible asset is its modeled tacit knowledge — the data model of internal processes — while the UI, chat surface, and general agent interaction commoditize. The strategic consequence: invest in the graph, and serve it into whatever agent surface users already inhabit.
data.name: The durable enterprise asset is modeled tacit knowledge; surfaces commoditize

data.brief: For single-cell foundation models, measurement realism and data quality gate generalization more than raw dataset scale — the opposite of the text-LLM "just scale it" story
data.name: Measurement quality gates single-cell generalization more than scale

data.brief: Review quality is a context property, not a capability property: the same class of model judges its own work generously and someone else's work honestly — architect the vantage (manager holds goals/history, workers hold implementation) instead of waiting for a less sycophantic model
data.name: Review quality is a context property, not a capability property

data.brief: Getting a proven prototype into production is a design problem in decomposition: the axes you slice a monolithic prototype along — informed by the RPT's type, persistence, and architecture mapping — determine whether the right subject-matter experts can review each slice and whether delivery dates are estimable; chronic timeline unpredictability is a downstream symptom of upstream legibility or repo problems
data.name: Getting a prototype into production is a design problem in decomposition

data.brief: The only way to replace the old cyber stack is through the models: with very high-quality evals, data, and benchmarks plus post-training, defenders can be made to out-perform attackers durably — because doing the exploitation leap fast and reliably is a lasting capability attackers don't uniquely have
data.name: Cyber defense must be model-native, built on evals, data, and post-training

data.brief: The leverage in embedded work is not proximity to the customer but control of the problem statement: customers describe solutions, so an FDE who redefines the problem, ships the small real fix before leaving the site and then articulates what comes next permanently owns the system and the narrative around it. Trust bought with bite-sized solved problems is what buys access to the real problem — which is the raw material for generalization (Foundry as the general product informed by tens of thousands of hours of exactly this). This, not social skill, is why FDEs matter in early sales.
data.name: Whoever defines the problem owns the solution

data.brief: Where no empirically correct answer exists (attribution credit), verification cannot be a truth-checker; it becomes structured deliberation — independent sampling by evidence-citing analysts plus a judge weighing reasoning quality, escalating by widening the jury. Extends the judge/verifier playbook beyond checkable outputs into judgment questions
data.name: Where no ground truth exists, verification becomes structured deliberation
