data.brief: The problems that decide whether an agentic product succeeds — snappy vs slow, all-at-once vs incremental, fragmented client versions — are delivery problems living between model output and screen, not model problems. A correct raw answer that leaves the user to do the work (the restaurant info dump vs a date-time-tap booking card) fails as a product even when the model "did the real work"
data.name: Delivery problems between model output and screen decide agentic products

data.brief: Point solutions cap out: automating prospecting inside sales, or AP inside finance, returns ~5-10% for that function, which is why so much deployed AI shows no measurable ROI. Transforming a whole department at once — classifying each step of an 8-step process as fully autonomous, human-in-the-loop, or human-only (risk too high, or too bespoke for an agent to add value) — is what produces the 25/50/75% numbers, denominated in the same three currencies the Cursor talk named: revenue uplift, cost savings, risk mitigation.
data.description: The binding design constraint is adoption, not capability: the new process must differ enough to capture the ROI but not so much that operators can't recognize it (replacing an 11-step workflow with one step gets handed back).
data.name: Department-wide re-engineering beats point solutions on ROI

data.brief: The field has enough defenses; it needs deployable ones. The frontier isn't a new attack-defense pair but making existing controls run at production overhead — an engineering problem. Research defends against invisible pixel tweaks while reality loses to stolen passwords and over-privileged accounts, and expertise silos (security doesn't speak ML, ML doesn't speak security, ops knows neither) leave the gap unowned
data.name: The field has enough defenses; it needs deployable ones

data.brief: The compounding trick of RSI: you are bottlenecked on the smartest model in your system, but that model creates the judges, reward models, and data generators for every loop — so each top-level improvement upgrades the entire training system at once, not just the product
data.name: Derivative models raise the intelligence floor of the whole training system

data.brief: Mimicking the human org chart (one agent per analyst step) is the anti-pattern: agent topology should be derived from observing what a capable agent naturally does with minimal tools, not from human role decomposition — judgment consolidates, investigation parallelizes
data.name: Derive agent topology from observed agent behavior, not the human org chart

data.brief: Design vertical AI for delegation, not participation: chat and citations are participation-era interfaces; the value unlock is long-running background agents wrapped in supervision surfaces (teach/monitor/control) — ask of every feature "what would delegating this look like?" rather than "how does the user do this here?"
data.name: Design vertical AI for delegation, not participation

data.brief: Sometimes the fix is neither a better model nor more oversight but the interaction itself: reframe the human as investigator rather than validator, require independent evidence, surface assumptions and trade-offs early, split compound questions (was the detection correct? vs. should we penalize? — headphones detected may be a hearing aid). Discernment is a designable property of the interface
data.name: Discernment is a designable property of the interface

data.brief: Safety evals should create real-world-shaped incentives (fraud pays if you get away with it) rather than prompting misbehavior, then measure what emerges — because deployed agents will meet exactly those incentives at mass scale, "especially when they're going to be much smarter than us very soon"
data.name: Safety evals should create real incentives and measure emergent misbehavior

data.brief: Path to no-touch automation: a deterministic rule engine resolves/flags everything it can first, agents handle only the residual reasoning, and a confidence gate decides human escalation — the automated share grows outward from the deterministic core
data.name: No-touch automation grows outward from a deterministic core, agents handle the residual

data.brief: The replay agent and pass@k are the same defect viewed twice: a deterministic environment can be beaten by a compiled tape of past successes, and any metric that rewards "at least one success in k tries" is measuring that tape. The fix is not a better metric on the same environments but variation with verified validity — which is expensive precisely because each generated configuration must be proven valid, the step raw coding-agent generation skips. Environment rigor and metric rigor are one problem: without stochasticity there is nothing for an honest interval to measure
data.name: Determinism is the exploit

data.brief: The hard part of agent video isn't authoring, it's determinism: browsers are async on purpose (fonts, images, assets load late) while video needs every pixel present on every frame; freezing the browser clock and seeking frame-by-frame converts the browser into a deterministic renderer — which is what upgrades "LLMs write web pages" into "anything a browser renders can ship as an MP4"
data.name: The hard part of agent video isn't authoring, it's determinism

data.brief: The reCAPTCHA architecture is the transferable lesson beyond CAPTCHAs: keep the loop deterministic and fast, and call the model only for the irreducible perception step, because anything that round-trips a model per action loses on latency and cost. It is the same detection-deterministic / investigation-agentic division the observability talks reached (Hylak, b19), arrived at independently under a hard time constraint — and it generalizes to any high-frequency browser task where a model-in-every-step harness is too slow and too expensive
data.name: Determinism with a vision oracle

data.brief: The clean division of labour that falls out of two of the talk's lessons is that detection should be deterministic and investigation agentic. Agents are unreliable at noticing that something is anomalous — they lack the baseline and the temporal frame — but effective once handed a concrete anomaly with a start time and a blast radius. Systems built the other way around, asking a model to surface what is wrong from raw traces, are asking for the half agents are worst at and skipping the half they are best at; clustering is the most common instance of that mistake
data.name: Deterministic detection agentic investigation

data.brief: A review-burden score must be deterministically computable from the PR + repo, never an LLM judge: judge-based scores are moving targets (same PR re-scores when the model changes) and indefensible in an engineering or leadership review — a number only changes behavior if it is traceable
data.name: Review-burden scores must be deterministic, never an LLM judge

data.brief: The developer job survives by moving up a level: from writing 100% of the code (linear, one-person progress) to designing the system the agents run within and applying judgment at review and merge — "scaling you, not replacing you"; the axe→chainsaw transition, and devs have always absorbed better tools
data.name: The developer job survives by moving up a level to system design

data.brief: The durable claim is temporal: general-purpose technologies take a generation to diffuse because adoption means ripping out equipment and retraining people, not because the technology is weak — so the binding constraint on AI's economic effect is deployment into firms that "still do things the same way," and the labs' capability curve is nearly irrelevant to it. Long Lake's answer (own the business, embed the product, show up) is the most extreme form of the corpus's FDE thesis
data.name: Diffusion is the bottleneck not capability

data.brief: Agentic systems have direct analogues for every classic engineering structure — skills ≈ packages, sub-agents ≈ functions ("good in any hood" because they don't carry session context), schemas ≈ API contracts, agents.md ≈ architecture docs — so engineers should apply existing instincts (code smells included) rather than treat agent design as alien
data.name: Agentic systems have direct analogues for every classic engineering structure

data.brief: Every boundary between training stages is a distribution discontinuity, and the discontinuities are where the damage happens: MoE experts imbalance when the post-training data looks nothing like pre-training; representations destabilize; capabilities are lost adapting to a domain. The remedy in every recipe examined is the same move in different directions — blur the boundary. Nemotron pulls SFT data backwards into pre-training; mid-training pulls the RL distribution and long context backwards ahead of post-training; and the curation-vendor account pushes the pre-training distribution forwards into mid-training to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
data.description: Two labs, opposite directions, same conclusion: the stage names are an artifact of team boundaries, and treating them as real is what costs you.
data.name: Every training-stage boundary is a distribution discontinuity where damage happens

data.brief: Both non-moderator panelists independently call the coming year "the most consequential year" for how AI gets distributed — not how capable it gets. The pieces: capability-level gating negotiated behind closed doors (the Fable/GPT-5.6 embargo), ~0.000001% of the 1–2B AI users ever having run an open model (target: 10–15%), on-device compute converging with open capability (day-to-day-capable model on a MacBook within the year; a 4B phone model already more useful than launch-day GPT-4), agent operating systems preloaded on hardware, and a September iPhone/Siri moment about to introduce local AI to the mass public the way DeepSeek did
data.name: Distribution is this years frontier question

data.brief: An agent's "I've implemented the new auth flow and it's all working perfectly" decodes to "to the best of my capabilities and of what you gave me, that sounds like it should work" — maybe it verified, maybe not; whether a user iterates on that gap or quits at the first false "done" is exactly the cleavage between AI maximalists and skeptics
data.name: An agent's "done" claim is a hypothesis, not a verified fact

data.brief: Two structural conflicts, one prescription each. For researchers: stop outsourcing your definition of realism to the same vendors you buy your evals and tasks from — that's letting the test writer grade the task. For builders: the moat is not the data, it is the pipeline into real-world work plus the infrastructure to keep retraining on it as the models improve underneath you — a dataset depreciates as the frontier moves, so only a live partnership is durable supply.
data.description: Corollary for vendors: environment companies that succeed are really research accelerators and the industry is boutique; it is venture-scalable only if the infrastructure they build in-house serves an enterprise app-layer use case, rather than assuming today's data market persists (his robotics counterexample: an unsettled modality — ego vs teleop vs UMI — entangles the vendor's choice with an unsolved research question, so don't die on a modality hill).
data.name: Don't buy your definition of realism from your eval vendor

data.brief: Krea's answer to constant silent failure is the same shape as the durable-execution thread elsewhere in the corpus: don't prevent the crash, make recovery cheap and automatic — frequent checkpoints on fast storage plus "mark the pod failed and let Kubernetes recreate it." The spot-arbitrage system extends the same logic to capacity: treat every GPU as preemptible, flip work between clusters, and let the scheduler self-heal. Reliability is engineered as cheap resume, not as uptime
data.name: Durability from cheap checkpoints

data.brief: The audience only ever sees the presentation mode; the editing format is invisible and therefore arbitrary — "slide deck" and "PowerPoint" are not synonyms. So pick the editing format agents are natively fluent in (HTML) and render to the human delivery format (PDF, PPT, MP4) as the last step; the tool-for-making-X and X itself decouple
data.name: The editing format is invisible and arbitrary; pick the one agents are fluent in

data.brief: The durable reframing: the enterprise's unit of adoption is not a model or a product but a *worker* — and the org already has a lifecycle for workers (register, provision, authorize, monitor, investigate, revoke). Treating agents as managed entities collapses "agent governance" into IT/HR practice moved down a layer, which is why the identity vendors (Microsoft, Okta, AWS) are the ones productizing it. What is genuinely new is only speed, scale and ambiguity
data.name: Employment readiness not capability

data.brief: Org-wide AI velocity was unlocked less by the models than by enablement machinery: per-role immersive training, security/processes/docs a non-engineer can follow, an internal knowledge MCP over decades of documentation, and engineers repositioned as teachers. The constraint on AI speed in a large org is human process change, not tool capability
data.name: Org-wide AI velocity was unlocked by enablement machinery, not the models

data.brief: Bespoke enforcement doesn't scale socially — it must become a language-agnostic, shareable contract ("given this task, fulfill this; the middle is developer-defined") that runs at every level: conversation end, pre-commit, multi-agent workflow steps, async agents, plus non-deterministic LLM-as-judge checks where needed
data.name: Bespoke enforcement must become a shareable, language-agnostic contract

data.brief: A verification loop is only as good as the engine powering it: an engine implementing ~50% of Excel's formulas is worse than none — the agent writes a correct formula, gets an engine error, and "fixes" what wasn't broken
data.name: A verification loop is only as good as the engine powering it

data.brief: The AI engineer's role inverts: instead of performing the dev loop (reading traces, hand-running evals, vibe-implementing fixes), you design loops with clear eval/termination gates and let agents work them autonomously in the background — spec-writing, gate-setting, and reviewing proposed changes become the human's judgment surface
data.name: The AI engineer's role inverts from performing the dev loop to designing loops

data.brief: Strip the checklist to its structure and enterprise readiness is a control plane: identity (SCIM-tied RBAC, entitlements), configuration (every admin setting via API, audited, rolled out deliberately), data boundaries (ZDR/CMEK, BYO gateway and infra, no training, transparent sub-processors) and a human on call. Vendors that ship this "from the beginning" clear an 8,000-person regulated fund and therefore "basically everybody else"; the same control plane is what the buyer must build internally before agents 100× its entitlement debt
data.name: Enterprise readiness is a control plane

data.brief: Where the environment stops is where the model stops. Agents write application code well because application work was captured — in repositories, issues and diffs — and reason poorly about MVCC and consensus because nobody ever recorded a decade of operating a cluster in a form a model could train on. So the unit of training data for autonomous engineering cannot be the diff; it has to be the company: the tickets and postmortems that explain why the last migration went wrong, the customer conversations that explain what "down" costs, the stale documentation the agent must notice is stale, the deployment system that conflicts with itself, and the live traffic that makes every choice carry a blast radius.
data.description: As long as the environment ends at the repository boundary, so does the model — and every benchmark on the current frontier ends there.
data.name: Where the environment stops is where the model stops

data.brief: For long-horizon agentic capability the lever has moved from model and data scale to environment design — formulating the problem, the reward, and the sandbox so that RL can iterate against a task that takes twelve hours and real GPUs. The same insight makes hacking a first-class engineering concern (multi-submission scoring, held-out validation) and makes a lab's internal, work-derived evals a private asset outsiders cannot replicate.
data.name: Environment design is the post-training lever for long-horizon capability

data.brief: Once compute, base models and training infrastructure are commodities, the scarce input keeps its identity but changes form: an RL environment is a dataset whose shape is executable. The practical consequence is that data-curation discipline transfers wholesale to environments — staged pipelines, per-stage ablations, quality measurement, versioning, and a scaling curve you prove before you scale spend — which is why the environment layer in the reference stack is a build/measure/version layer, not a content library.
data.name: An RL environment is a dataset whose shape is executable

data.brief: Deployment change-management heuristic, via Walt Disney's Epcot — conceived as a master-planned exemplary city, landed as a theme park, yet real cities still copied its transit ideas. A reference implementation has to be advanced enough that people say "let's bring that to my part of the codebase", but not so advanced that they say "that's a theme park, that has nothing to do with how we work".
data.description: Building two or three exemplars at that calibration and letting the customer's own team scale them out is the transformation mechanism; overshooting triggers cost-of-change panic instead of adoption.
data.name: Calibrate reference implementations so customers copy them rather than dismiss them

data.brief: Because generative AI regresses to the training-set mean, human judgment has a specific new job: supplying the non-average direction — naming whose problem is being solved, what winning looks like, and which decision should change. Without that steering, AI-accelerated teams just ship the existing world faster
data.name: Human judgment's new job is supplying the non-average direction

data.brief: The eval is not a fixed measuring stick held against a moving agent — the two hill-climb together. When a run misses the bar, the correct move may be to review the eval set, recompute precision/recall, adjust the rating guide, change the tooling, or change the agent; all five are moves in the same loop. The corollary is that an eval built too early and frozen becomes a brake on architecture change, which is why the deliberately non-scalable phase comes first and the comprehensive suite comes after the failure patterns are understood.
data.name: The eval and the agent hill-climb together rather than one measuring the other

data.brief: Production traces look free — you get them anyway, you never pay to author them — but they are paid for in two currencies teams don't price: every test runs on live users, and experiments serialize because production has one timeline. Simulation converts eval data from a harvested scarce resource into a manufactured on-demand one, and that conversion, not any model improvement, is what unlocks high-throughput experimentation. The corollary that makes it work for agents specifically: the expensive part of an agent data point is trajectory-wide state consistency, which a simulator can guarantee and a hand-author cannot.
data.name: Eval data becomes manufactured on demand instead of harvested from production

data.brief: A too-easy eval (90% pass off polite simulated users) is a warning sign, not a win: realistic difficulty (real-verbatim-tuned users, adversarial personas — bypasser, refund-seeker, AI-skeptic) lowers scores but is the only way an offline eval predicts production and leaves room to improve the agent against hard users; scores only matter when they gate a decision (launch gates, regression gates with clear owners)
data.name: A too-easy eval is a warning sign, not a win

data.brief: "You can't improve what you can't measure": guardrails, evaluation (pre-ship) and monitoring (post-ship) are one continuous discipline for probabilistic systems — without measured guardrail-compliance, faithfulness, and domain metrics you can't even investigate failures; production adds implicit indicators (human-override rate, review duration) that no offline eval captures
data.name: You can't improve what you can't measure — eval and monitoring are one discipline

data.brief: A simple eval gate does not make a system safe. A learning loop can. The durable artifact is not the passing test or the one edge case that got fixed — it is the pipeline that converts a traced production moment into an expert annotation, the annotation into a typed eval with a replayable turn index, and the eval into a CI gate.
data.description: That is what makes an entire risk category lift at once and every subsequent prompt, model and guardrail change get scored against accumulated expert judgment. The corollary the speakers draw is against benchmark maximization: chasing a perfect score drifts attention away from the humans the benchmark exists to protect.
data.name: An eval gate does not make a system safe; a learning loop can

data.brief: Eval infrastructure generalizes into a distributed agent runtime. Once you can run any agent with any model in any sandbox on any task, evaluation is just one consumer: the same engine does agentic map-reduce over a corpus, and the loop closes — mining your own agent sessions for recurring mistakes produces the feedback that defines the next batch of eval tasks, which in turn picks a better agent or trains a better scaffold. Harbor's builders learned this from users rather than designing it, then shipped for it
data.name: Eval infrastructure generalizes into a distributed agent runtime

data.brief: Running auto-research is like training a model: your eval is the data + loss function (the environment the agent trains against). Proprietary evaluation data and unique domain judgment about what to measure become a vertical moat that gets amplified as auto-research strengthens
data.name: In auto-research the eval is the data plus loss function — and a vertical moat

data.brief: Where an eval can sit is a function of how fast it runs, so latency is a first-class eval design constraint rather than an implementation detail: a slow committee of frontier judges can only grade after the fact, while a ~3-second judge can sit inside the generation loop and catch drift at the frame where fixing it is cheapest. Distillation is not a quality play here — it is what buys the placement, and the choice between committee and distilled model is decided on unit economics.
data.name: Eval latency decides where an eval can sit, making it a design constraint

data.brief: Owning the eval that matters converts model choice from a trust/brand decision into a commodity procurement decision on the cost/performance Pareto frontier; the eval, not the model relationship, is the durable asset ("as soon as you have an eval the power is now in your hands")
data.name: The eval, not the model relationship, is the durable asset

data.brief: Complete eval suites cannot be authored up front — domain experts can't pre-guess all criteria or edge cases; real suites are discovered: every production failure becomes a new detection eval plus a remedy, new criteria flow back into the spec, and the agent's eval suite compounds with usage — the more production data seen, the better-scoring the agent
data.name: Complete eval suites cannot be authored up front — they are discovered

data.brief: Eval methods accrete rather than replace: deterministic evals, LLM-as-judge, and agent-as-judge are different tools for different problem shapes, and the correct selector is trajectory variance. Fixed rubrics work where the flow is deterministic and failures are enumerable; adaptive agentic analysis is required where every run takes a different path and the interesting failures (loops, wasted tool calls, no done-detection) are only visible across the whole trajectory. The corollary is that evals belong on live production traces — that is where the data for continual-learning loops comes from — not only in an offline suite.
data.name: Eval tiers accrete rather than replace; trajectory variance selects the tier

data.brief: Evals and environments are the same artifact: building evals for model min-maxing (Opus vs Sonnet vs GPT, intelligence vs dollars) already produces the unit needed for post-training — so eval investment opens a flywheel where your custom model keeps improving on real-world signal alongside the frontier, with training compute amortized as a small fraction of inference spend
data.name: Evals and environments are the same artifact, opening a post-training flywheel

data.brief: The durable claim inverts the usual hierarchy: models and architectures are transient (each release forces a re-platform), so the one artifact that persists is the eval suite — the executable description of how the system is supposed to behave — and it must be re-fitted to each architecture or it silently measures the wrong system. Verification is the continuity layer through generational change
data.name: Evals are the durable asset across replatforms

data.brief: The record/playback eval harness was the unlock that made every later refactor safe: quality went from anecdote ("manual tests on production data that gets retentioned away") to a graded regression suite — without it you cannot know whether changes broke earlier wins
data.name: The record/playback eval harness made every later refactor safe

data.brief: Evals for a graph-backed agent debug the data model, not just the agent: failures surface gaps, ambiguities, and reporting-standard mismatches in the model itself; residual misses are typically "right but not what the user intended" (ambiguity), not wrong. Graph modeling likewise exposes the developer's unknown unknowns — gaps in understanding and un-ingested datasets — making the modeling process valuable in itself.
data.name: Evals for graph-backed agents debug the data model, not just the agent

data.brief: As models saturate simulations and detect them, real-life deployments become the load-bearing eval — messy and N=1, but rich in behavioral signal about which models actually perform out of distribution; real-to-sim forking recovers reproducibility (replay any incident across models), getting the best of both worlds
data.name: Real-world deployments become the load-bearing eval as models saturate simulations

data.brief: SWE-bench-style evals ("does the code run and produce the right output") measure a small slice of engineering; benchmarks need open-ended, never-saturating problems with scalar loss functions — e.g. lossless text compression scored as compressed size + source size — that force genuinely novel algorithms; relatedly, chain-of-code reasoning should extend to spatial/dynamic (multimodal) thinking, since code-writing is a visual activity for humans
data.name: Evals need open-ended, never-saturating problems with scalar loss functions

data.brief: Capability skills are depreciating assets — temporary patches over model gaps, retired surprisingly fast as models update ("needed six months ago, not today"); the eval is the durable asset: keep it after retiring the skill, use it to detect degradation, and reintroduce the skill only when the eval says so. Run ablations (with/without skill) to know which regime you're in
data.name: Capability skills are depreciating assets; the eval is the durable asset

data.brief: An event-sourced system arrives pre-fitted for agents: it already holds immutable, time-ordered business facts, already has a propagation mechanism (CDC / change feed / broker), and already builds purpose-shaped read models. Adopting agents therefore reduces to adding one more projection — an agent-facing semantic layer — rather than to adopting a memory product. The corollary is the portability claim the speaker makes explicitly: any event source and either a relational or NoSQL store will do, and teams that don't practise event sourcing can reach the same place via the message broker.
data.name: An event-sourced system is already agent-ready context

data.brief: Production verification is escaping the pipeline: instead of a fixed battery of checks authored in advance, each change event gets a verification plan generated *for it* — derived from the change's content, scoped to its causal chain, scheduled on its risk profile — and change paths that never had verification (feature flags, infra edits) get it for free. Combined with confidence-gated human confirmation (the agent DMs before it answers publicly), this inverts on-call: the always-on agent watches continuously and the human becomes the escalation path, rather than the pager being the system's first responder
data.name: Every change gets a bespoke verifier

data.brief: One primitive underlies the whole agent-development loop: task → sandbox → agent → trajectory → verifier → reward, aggregated across a dataset. "Take off the mask" and evals and RL training data are the same object — environments — so a single rollout engine serves benchmarking, sellable task data, SFT on trajectories, RL on trajectory tokens + rewards, text-feedback optimization, and plain production batch work. The loop looks simple but is "extremely universal", with flavors (multi-step, separate verification sandbox, artifacts, simulated users) layered on the same bare-bones skeleton
data.name: Evals and RL training data are the same object — one rollout primitive underlies both

data.brief: Her closing thesis: product engineering, agent engineering, AI engineering, solutions engineering and customer engineering are all trending toward forward deployed engineering, because enablement, DevOps, solution building, data integration and shipping an agent into production are all ultimately performed on behalf of a customer and should be priced against the outcome they produce. The discipline's incoherent definition is therefore not a problem to fix but the sign of a merge — "forward deployed engineering is dead; long live forward deployed engineering".
data.name: Every adjacent engineering discipline is converging on forward deployed engineering

data.brief: Enterprise documentation describes the golden path and maybe one edge case; the operational truth is the exception route — who it goes to when it breaks and how many days that costs — and it is different at every company. That undocumented layer, not model capability, is why agents can't run enterprise processes end to end, which makes "what happens when things go wrong?" the highest-yield question an FDE asks and makes the resulting dependency graph (with its cycles and its real owners) the actual deliverable of the discovery phase. Storage is incidental; reliable traversal is the hard problem, and it is worth an RL environment of its own.
data.name: The undocumented exception paths are the context enterprise agents lack

data.brief: The talk's task decomposition is a market claim: with capable models, the execution half of any ops task (load the dashboard, run the check, call the tool) is commodity — what's scarce is production context, the learned, environment-specific judgment that a metric "feels wrong" before anyone can articulate why. That is why an ops-agent vendor's differentiation lives in the learning/knowledge system rather than the model, why the models slide is one bullet and the learning slide gets the "we spend so much time here", and why the sellable interface (MCP) exports *learned context*, not model access. The ops-agent market is a context market
data.name: Execution is commodity context is the product

data.brief: The execution layer sits between user input and everything the system does — user feedback, actions, and session results all flow through it — making it the natural hub for full-stack traces and for outcome-based agent scoring ("did the triage lead to an engineering action?", "was the PR opened?", "was the report saved?") instead of thumbs-up/thumbs-down
data.name: Execution layer is the hub for full traces and outcome-based scoring

data.brief: Fidelity is a relation between an output and a documentary record, so no automated metric operating on the model alone can adjudicate it — the metric cannot see the archive. A domain expert (historian, classicist, theologian, clinical psychologist) in the evaluation loop is a structural technical requirement, not a courtesy: "a persona system without a domain expert in its evaluation loop is a thermometer that cannot read temperature" (paraphrase)
data.name: Fidelity needs a domain expert in the evaluation loop

data.brief: The mechanism by which a domain-expert organization injects proprietary knowledge into a self-improving system is neither prompt engineering nor context stuffing — it is environment construction. The verifiable metric is "maybe the easy part"; the expertise lives in the qualitative rubric that grades a rollout on process (what a good quant researcher actually does), because that is the signal the model then learns from. This inverts the usual enterprise-AI posture: the institution stops guarding its harness and starts guarding its measurement surface.
data.name: Institutional expertise encodes as environments and rubrics, not prompts

data.brief: The durable organizational claim is the division of labor: the expert owns the *what* (the procedure, its exceptions, its evidence), the agent owns the *how*, and the engineering is the translation layer between them — making work representable, execution bounded, behavior observable, correction cheap, improvement compounding. The "AI-native operation" here is not agents in a workflow but a methodology whose main asset is the corrected, country-aligned process memory
data.name: Experts own the what agents own the how

data.brief: Operational rule for AI-era shipping: explain it or don't ship it — not because humans type or read every line, but because someone must understand the work well enough to defend it; the owners-file model (named humans on the hook per subsystem) generalizes to agent output
data.name: Explain it or don't ship it: someone must understand the work well enough to defend it

data.brief: Horthy/Pstrucha's core delta: a software factory can run mechanical, spec'd, test-covered slices unattended, but it cannot honestly decide whether it built the right thing — architecture, trade-offs, and what-not-to-build stay human ("agents love complexity; they will keep adding to the stack unbounded"); Horthy: full lights-off slop-free looping is solvable only at the model level, not in the harness
data.name: A software factory cannot decide whether it built the right thing

data.brief: The rule for real-time agents: pick the fastest model your latency budget allows, then spend the rest of your effort on scaffolding — for voice/real-time/high-volume systems the model is the smallest part of the system
data.name: Pick the fastest model your latency budget allows, then spend on scaffolding

data.brief: FDE creates value only in the band between the extremes of customer digital maturity × product customizability: high-maturity/low-customization → self-serve docs; low/low → traditional SaaS rollout; high/high → advisers who accelerate. Misplaced FDE degenerates into staff augmentation, bores away your 10x engineers, and they leave
data.name: FDE creates value only in the middle band of maturity × customizability

data.brief: Because the role's jobs-to-be-done accumulated rather than rotated, "what vintage of FDE are you?" resolves a title that otherwise conveys nothing — a 2008-vintage FDE (platform stability) and a 2024-vintage FDE (agent building against customer outcomes) share only customer accountability. The same accumulation explains the Palantir alumni founder pipeline: the role is generalist training across every layer of delivering software to a customer, which is exactly the profile the market now bids for.
data.name: Asking which vintage of FDE someone is resolves a title that otherwise conveys nothing

data.brief: The standardized environment format has a physical ceiling, and it is reached sooner than the field assumes. A single containerized node can fake a surprising amount — multiple cluster members, flapping nodes, lagging learners, even live traffic — and deterministic simulation can fake network partitions, but neither can fake provisioning: the moment the task involves creating a host, a VPC, a security group or a customer-facing API with throttling and audit logging, the simulation stops being a simulation of the thing and starts being a different thing.
data.description: That pushes environments toward provisioning real cloud resources, which imports real costs into training: an AWS-Lambda-scale stack takes hours to stand up against a rollout budget measured in minutes, and the bill is real. And the honest close is that it does not even close the gap — with real infrastructure you still have no live customer traffic and none of the problems that only appear at scale.
data.name: Environment fidelity is a budget you spend, and the last increment is unpurchasable

data.brief: Every rung of post-training is the same trade in a different costume: the more of the setup you move outside your training stack, the more real it gets and the less you can learn from it. In-stack Q&A gives you total control of format and a clean gradient, and teaches nothing about multi-turn work. A synthetic environment buys long horizons and replayability, and charges you the fidelity gap — the agent will faithfully learn your 10% tool-call failure rate and your timeout filter along with the task.
data.description: The real harness removes the fidelity gap entirely and takes replayability, on-policy data and comparative reward with it. There is no rung where you get both, which is why the frontier work is all about extracting a gradient from data you cannot re-run.
data.name: Every post-training rung trades realism against the signal you can learn from

data.brief: The deployed-engineering org is the vendor's best evaluation set: "we have the highest fidelity evaluation set that comes back from our customers — we are in the field every single day". Solving the customer's problem completely is only half the equation; the other half is carrying that context back so the product moves toward the customers' problems, maximizing the overlap of the two circles (what we build x what they need).
data.description: Enterprise engineering challenges arrive "in similar shapes", so the field job is classification — is this challenge common across the enterprise or unique to this user, and should this workaround, hack or bug become a feature? — and the payoff is a de-risked roadmap where you know what to build for which revenue. The feedback is "half of the loop that makes the next deployment better than the previous deployment".
data.name: The deployed-engineering org is the vendor's highest-fidelity evaluation set

data.brief: You cannot out-review generated code, and the amount of unread code in your codebase only goes up from here — so the leverage moves down a layer, into the substrate the code is written in. A compiler that infers and proves error handling, CI that fails on a violated architectural invariant, a trace on every file, and a symbol description that answers in one call are all the same move: making unread code safe rather than making more of it read.
data.description: Followed to its end, the argument indicts the whole foundation — languages, Git, databases were designed to maximize human productivity, and every system built on them inherits the compromises. The talk's ask is that the bravest of the audience go rebuild those layers for agent authors.
data.name: You cannot out-review generated code, so the leverage moves into the substrate

data.brief: For a single task, a synthetic dataset plus a fine-tune does not buy a few points of accuracy — it buys an entire device class. A 270M-500M model fine-tuned on 10K-10M synthetic samples matches or beats a 2-4B general model on that task while reaching older laptops, low-tier browsers, IoT boards and consumer robots that the small tier cannot run on at all, and while being several times more responsive because there is less to read from memory per step.
data.description: The remaining friction is the dataset, not the model — which is why having an agent generate the synthetic data for you is the stated route to making this playbook available to far more people.
data.name: A fine-tune on synthetic data buys an entire device class

data.brief: Token-cost optimization has a 90/10 structure: output-side tricks (short answers, max-tokens settings) cap out at single-digit total savings; the real lever is input-side context selection. "We argue about which model is best, Opus or Sonnet — but the model may be 30% of the cost; the other 70% is what you feed it. Fix the input; the model choice matters less than you think" (paraphrase)
data.name: Token-cost optimization is 90/10: input-side context selection is the lever

data.brief: A multi-machine agent fleet re-derives classic distributed systems one outage at a time: state sync, credential isolation, scheduling, node failure, a single control plane. The four problems still open (cross-machine consistency, local-only tools like MCP servers/browser, secure credential handoff, resource placement) are exactly the questions Kubernetes already answers — so the emerging shape is Kubernetes-style infra underneath, agent-native orchestration (task routing, review flow, context management) on top, rather than reinventing compute/secrets/tools
data.name: Multi-machine agent fleets re-derive classic distributed systems problems

data.brief: Agents dissolve SaaS-era friction moats (integrations, switching costs — gone when an agent rewrites 100K–1M lines Python→Rust in days); the replacement moat is *fluency*: how fast an arriving agent picks up your platform's operational knowledge. "Teachability" joins security/compliance/SLA on the enterprise evaluation checklist, and skills are the commoditization vehicle for that experience layer
data.name: Agents dissolve SaaS moats; the new moat is platform fluency

data.brief: The talk's durable lesson is that context economics are governed by *frequency*, not volume: a rented query costs the same on the thousandth ask as the first even when the answer is unchanged, so any workload that revisits the same entities repeatedly (due diligence, monitoring, market research) crosses a build-beats-rent tipping point far sooner than intuition suggests. That reframes agent-context procurement as an amortization decision, and it generalizes past web data to any external context an agent queries on a cadence — the same owned-vs-rented calculus the memory-compute-budget talks reached (Khemani, b19)
data.name: Frequency is the hidden cost axis

data.brief: Once generation is hours-long and parallel, the constraint moves out of engineering: deciding what to build and approving its launch — previously noise against a year of coding — now dominate, and the human costs (flowmaxxing, review load on juniors, leaders' impatience) accrue where the old process assumed slack. The corpus's judgement thesis observed as an operating constraint inside a 2,000-team scale-out
data.name: Frontier teams relocate the long pole to decisions

data.brief: Claude Code enables cloning cloud apps locally. Not data portability — functionality portability. Apps without network effects are easy to clone.
data.description: The "file over app" philosophy (Kepano/Obsidian) argued that files are portable but apps are not. The new information as of 2026: apps are suddenly portable too. Claude Code enables rapid cloning of moderately complex cloud applications into local equivalents. This isn't data portability — it's functionality portability. Any SaaS application of moderate complexity without strong global network effects is now vulnerable to being cloned locally. The moat was never the feature set — it was the assumption that rebuilding was prohibitively expensive. That assumption has collapsed.
data.importance: Explains why SaaS moat was never the feature set — it was the rebuild cost. That cost is now near-zero.
data.name: Functionality is now portable

data.brief: At 70% agent-written PRs the remaining bottlenecks are physical and human: CI capacity, experiment slots, reviewer attention (hence inner-loop validation, tiered review, throttled maintenance loops) and the decision of what to build. Uber's factory is the corpus's verification-gap and judgement theses observed as operating constraints rather than predictions
data.name: Generation solved capacity and judgement remain

data.brief: The generator cannot be its own validator — self-review finds half the issues, inconsistently; independence (and determinism) is the load-bearing property
data.name: The generator cannot be its own validator

data.brief: The durable lesson is that the fix for an LLM that "reinvents the wheel every time" is not a better prompt but a domain-intent vocabulary layer the model applies over deterministic systems — tags the engine executes, described in the language the user already thinks in. That is the harness-over-model thesis in a specific form: the reliability comes from the tag substrate and the LOD context assembly, not the model's intelligence, and it generalizes to any tool where users have a rich domain vocabulary (game design, video editing, music) that the raw engine primitives don't expose
data.name: Give the model a domain vocabulary

data.brief: The golden dataset is the load-bearing artifact of agent development — baseline, regression suite, and optimizer objective in one; a live-data loop that converts production failures into golden-dataset entries turns user pain into a compounding verification asset
data.name: The golden dataset is the load-bearing artifact of agent development

data.brief: Steering context has a Goldilocks zone: too little and the model goes off the rails, too much and quality degrades — keep agents.md/CLAUDE.md-style always-on files down to the rules that matter, and move on-demand knowledge into keyword-activated skills that load only when triggered
data.name: Steering context has a Goldilocks zone

data.brief: A knowledge graph's highest-leverage use for agents is not retrieval but control: encoding the hypothesis space as edges gives the agent a bounded, expert-validated investigation surface — the graph decides what the agent may consider next
data.name: A knowledge graph's highest-leverage agent use is control, not retrieval

data.brief: Graph memory gives developers a convergence loop vector memory lacks: a wrong answer is introspectable — look at the returned subgraph, see exactly which context produced the answer, fix the extraction, merge duplicate nodes — so quality improves iteratively instead of remaining a black-box similarity score.
data.name: Graph memory is introspectable — wrong answers become a convergence loop

data.brief: Graph-native algorithms deliver retrieval capabilities that vector search cannot: PPR finds important nodes in dense clusters, shortest paths explain relationships between two known nodes (and citation chains to landmark cases never directly cited), and subgraph matching finds things by shape with no known instance — an enabling class, not an optimization
data.name: Graph-native algorithms deliver retrieval capabilities vector search cannot

data.brief: The graph representation earns its keep through localization and explanation: knowing WHICH node deviated and WHAT kind of drift it is turns raw telemetry into an actionable, explainable decision — "your health score is 22" from a doctor means nothing without the underlying data. It is the same move context graphs make for agents — structure as the understanding layer — applied to system behavior instead of knowledge.
data.name: Graphs earn their keep by localizing which node deviated and what kind of drift

data.brief: Similarity search can only match what exists; the differentiated value of graph context is estate-level reasoning — proving something is missing, finding unused documentation, surfacing mismatches between documented procedure and field reality.
data.name: Graph context's differentiated value is estate-level reasoning and proving negatives

data.brief: Bolting AI onto a SaaS-era GTM stack cannot scale: stand-alone AI can't infer buyer role/history/intent, old stacks can't capture the signals AI generates, and the architecture itself must be rebuilt with a per-buyer context graph at the core — solving identity and integration without the architecture still fails. The greeting test makes it visible: a bolted-on chat asks "how can I help you?" to a late-stage buyer who already decided, and they walk
data.name: Bolting AI onto a SaaS-era GTM stack cannot scale

data.brief: An agentic system's read surface is unbounded and adversarial by default, so input filtering is the wrong control point — it either lets attacks through or gates everything and destroys the agent's usefulness. The tractable control point is the action: a small, fast, deterministic decision at the moment of effect, with a learned model layered on top for the evasions determinism cannot see. The corollary that makes this urgent is compositional: the units being audited (skills) are individually clean, so audit-per-unit is structurally blind and only runtime, effect-level checks can see the attack.
data.name: Guard the effect, not the input

data.brief: For agents that run while you sleep, safety properties must be properties of the *system*, not requests to the model: any rule expressed as a prompt is one injection away from gone, so the real guardrails are declarative and deterministic — enumerated writes (including "nothing"), allowlisted egress, secrets held by a warden outside the jail, staged writes, total logging. This is what makes unsupervised background automation shippable at platform scale: trust re-architected into scaffolding the model cannot talk its way past. The industrial-revolution corollary: automation only compounds into bought-back time for craft when nobody has to babysit it
data.name: Guardrails outside the prompt

data.brief: The leadership operating model that emerges — automated guards (budgets, quotas, anomalies), regular contextual human review of the dashboards feeding institutional knowledge, and a loop where leaders and individuals refine the guardrails together — is the same three-part shape as the batch's spend-governance tooling (attribute, ledger, steer) rendered as management practice; with the smoke-detector rule as the cultural guard against token maxing
data.name: Guards review and a learning loop

data.brief: Why cybersecurity fits reinforcement learning better than most domains: it decomposes into a ladder of tasks with a good oracle at every rung, which is exactly how elite human hackers are trained — graduated difficulty, study write-ups, emulate, climb. Designing an RL curriculum for security is therefore pedagogy design along two axes (target difficulty and exploitation difficulty), not a modelling problem; the same methodology that took a 17-year-old from picoCTF to a Pwn2Own win in two years is what is being applied to frontier models.
data.name: Hacking is a ladder, which is why cybersecurity fits RL

data.brief: Each agent hallucination class has a deterministic code-level fix, not a prompt-level one: token waste → semantic tool filtering; fabricated aggregates → graph queries that compute; fabricated success → a separate validator; ignored rules → hooks the model cannot escape; over-blocking → runtime steering that lets the agent self-correct (split 6 guests into two rooms) instead of hard-stopping. "Each one is a code change, not a prompt change"; hard constraints get hooks, soft constraints get steering
data.name: Each agent hallucination class has a code-level fix, not a prompt-level one

data.brief: Hallucination is not a pre-training defect. Pre-training is "phenomenal" — compressing the internet into a core of intelligence that can then be utilized — and pre-trained models are "incredibly intelligent"; the problem is how we unearth it. The reward model's asymmetry does the damage: uncertainty is cheap to detect and punish, confidence is not, so the optimization drops modes and rewards sounding right. That makes overpromising a designed-in property of every RLHF model, and it means no matter how wrong the models are, they will look right — the exact failure that forces trust to be re-architected outside the model.
data.name: Hallucination is an artifact of the preference objective, not a pre-training defect

data.brief: Hallucination is the feature, not the bug — probabilistic imagination is what LLMs are (as it is for humans, who imagine things and then make them real). The fix is not eliminating it inside the model but pairing the neural generator with a symbolic validator outside it: reasoner-backed guardrails keep the LLM honest while preserving what makes it useful.
data.name: Hallucination is the feature — pair the neural generator with a symbolic validator

data.brief: Every handoff between skills is a place the system can lie to you, and solo builders have no second pair of eyes. Risk-rank handoffs by cost — a wrong claim published publicly, a schema break cascading to three skills, a duplicate that erodes audience trust — not by complexity, and gate the most expensive one first
data.name: Every handoff is where the system can lie; gate the most expensive first

data.brief: The durable finding is a boundary on autonomous research: given a real benchmark where success requires reasoning about a handful of hardware trade-offs, frontier models reproduce the patterns they have seen and stall on the ones they haven't — even with the trade-offs supplied — and an agent harness moves the number once, not continuously. The corpus's accelerated-research thesis gets a measured counter at exactly the layer (interconnect-bound kernels) where the next efficiency gains live
data.name: Hardware tradeoff reasoning is where models stop

data.brief: Process guarantees and task capability are separate axes: the harness makes even wrong answers safe, inspectable, and correctable (reject/retry loops; review artifacts non-coders can validate), while prompts, few-shot examples, and tool ergonomics raise first-pass accuracy. You need both — guarantees don't substitute for hill-climbing, and accuracy doesn't substitute for guarantees when ground truth is itself one point on a range of expert judgments
data.name: Process guarantees and task capability are separate axes; you need both

data.brief: In adaptive engineering the harness flips from input to output: agents form, specialize, cluster, and converge on conventions the way birds form a flock — identity is the position an agent takes relative to others, boundaries are drawn by the system, governance emerges without a governor; the engineer keeps only the constraint dials (enable/govern, reward/cost, coupling rate) and a sense-and-respond posture
data.name: In adaptive engineering the harness flips from input to output

data.brief: The context-anxiety story is the cleanest statement anyone has given of why harness engineering is structurally unlike ordinary infrastructure work: every workaround is a bet about a model deficiency, and the bet expires when the deficiency does — silently, while continuing to cost latency and cache efficiency. That makes harness code a depreciating asset requiring scheduled re-examination rather than a foundation that accrues value, and it explains why the vendor's own answer is to sell the harness as a managed service. It also sets the design rule the talk states outright: build for the model capabilities of *tomorrow*, and keep components independently swappable so the architecture survives what the model stops needing
data.name: Harness code is a depreciating asset

data.brief: When a lab open-sources its harness *and* pushes that harness's best features into an openly-governed inference protocol, it is conceding that the harness is not the moat — and simultaneously making the protocol the place where lock-in can still accrue. The interesting competitive surface stops being "whose agent is better" and becomes whose API shape the ecosystem standardizes on: tool search, patch semantics, compaction format and transport are all decisions that, once adopted by third-party runtimes, are far stickier than any agent UI
data.name: Harness differentiation migrates to protocol

data.brief: "The model is useless" in isolation: open and closed models are broadly comparable — measured differences come from the harness (Claude Code vs Codex vs a benchmark's control harness swings SWE accuracy 40%→50%, Gemini CLI 20%→40%), the system prompt, and the serving stack; small open models' tool-calling failures are likewise a harness problem more than a capability ceiling
data.name: Models are comparable; measured differences come from harness, prompt, and serving

data.brief: Agent leverage is gated on the guardrail stack, not model choice: agents are "toddlers" oscillating between genius and dumb, so constrain them like untrusted contractors — AGENTS.md intent, skill contracts ("do not improvise logic"), tool allowlists, sandboxes, and PR approval gates; 20× more code without guardrails is just 20× more slop
data.name: Agent leverage is gated on the guardrail stack, not model choice

data.brief: If harness quality can substitute for model quality (HarnessBench's 20-point spread, largest for weak models), the industry's dependency structure flips: cutting-edge agent performance stops being gated on a handful of frontier labs, and local/open-source models become viable for serious agent work — harness expertise is the sovereignty lever
data.name: Harness expertise is the sovereignty lever

data.brief: Against "as models get better, the harness disappears": predictive world model (priors) and experiential world model (the event log) are complements, not stages — like humans, an agent is not its reasoning capability but the beliefs, knowledge, and behaviors derived from lived experience, with the log feeding priors through replay/sleep. The agent's identity lives in its own log; we need both.
data.name: Predictive and experiential world models are complements; identity lives in the log

data.brief: A reference hierarchy (index summaries → per-source executive summary → wiki derivative → full raw source) means the agent usually stops early and reads the expensive full source only as a last resort — token efficiency achieved through file structure and referencing instead of retrieval infrastructure; executive summaries are computed once at ingestion and amortized forever
data.name: A reference hierarchy buys token efficiency through file structure

data.brief: Human-in-the-loop is only a control if the approval itself is policy-gated: the approver must hold the role for the action, so a consent-fatigued 2am "approve" from the wrong human is rejected by the same policy engine
data.name: Human-in-the-loop is only a control if the approval itself is policy-gated

data.brief: The title's argument, generalized: once sub-agent parallelism is cheap, the constraint migrates from model capability to the orchestrator's attention. Fifty parallel agents do not make a team fifty times faster if a person must watch them; the cost surface becomes windows, monitors and context switches (hence a metric as blunt as neck rotations per shipped change). Two responses follow, and they are different in kind: collapse the orchestration surface into one pane, and remove the human from the middle of the loop while keeping them at its boundary — because the boundary role is verification, which is not a throughput function.
data.name: Human attention becomes the ceiling once sub-agent parallelism is cheap

data.brief: Each software era was shaped by its binding constraint: machine power (assembly era), then the human brain — modular design, libraries, and abstraction exist because humans hold ~7–9 tokens of working memory; with model context effectively infinite, that constraint dissolves, and with it much of why software engineering is organized the way it is. Humans keep the roles the model lacks: specifying what is actually wanted, and inductive/cross-domain pattern transfer
data.name: Software structure exists for human working memory; that constraint dissolves

data.brief: Automating review does not remove the human; it changes what the human reviews. Agents in the loop need a *higher* accuracy bar than humans (cavitation), auto-landing is near, and the quality that makes either possible was learned from human feedback — so the outer loop is expanded upward to architecture, domain and product rather than deleted. The review-becomes-governance thread (Aviator, Warp, Qodo, Anthropic, Uber's SDLC) now has its operator-side statement
data.name: Human review moves up a layer because feedback was the signal

data.brief: Agentic GTM systems die at human trust boundaries, not model quality: flag everything hot and reps stop acting (alert fatigue); let AI-drafted emails need >30 seconds of editing and reps go back to writing their own. Survival = context-graph-throttled alerts + near-send-ready drafts + a policy engine the GTM operator (not a developer) can audit and fix
data.name: Agentic GTM systems die at human trust boundaries, not model quality

data.brief: The argument that non-replayable learning must be possible is empirical, not theoretical: a human in that same customer-support chat learns from the customer's reaction without ever running a counterfactual — they "internalize improvements for the future" from a single trajectory they cannot rewind. So the obstacle is not that the data is uninformative; it is that the field's current method requires a luxury production never provides — many parallel rollouts of the same prompt for relative comparison. Read that way, self-distillation, automated trace triage and qualitative-feedback ingestion are not three tricks but three attempts at the same missing algorithm.
data.name: Humans learn from single unrepeatable trajectories, so the missing piece is the algorithm

data.brief: Data quality is the lever: finding out-of-distribution zero-days still needs human vulnerability researchers; humans discover novel exploits in widely-used open-source software, which become deterministically-graded black-box environments used to post-train models to reason (not pattern-match) across an entire attack surface
data.name: Humans find out-of-distribution zero-days; models scale the exploitation

data.brief: Karpathy's ~2015 "gradient descent can write code better than you" is the metaphor for auto-research now: it commoditizes execution skills while making higher-level skills — creativity, eval design, abstraction design, driving the systems themselves — exponentially more valuable. The search is automated; humans move up the stack, not out of it. Community/competition designers gain huge leverage
data.name: Auto-research commoditizes execution; humans move up the stack, not out

data.brief: In agentic science, implementation is "already quite solved" (especially in simulatable environments) and memory/learning is an organization problem; the true bottleneck is hypothesis generation — so the leverage point is scaffolding that makes a reasoning model enumerate and attack every component of the problem, i.e. a structured way to scale test-time compute on the problem
data.name: Hypothesis generation is the true bottleneck of agentic science

data.brief: "Idea velocity" = humans compress to intent (brief Slack messages, frictionless communication) while a layered stack — manager with memory → orchestrator → workers → sub-agents — absorbs implementation; the human's residual job is judgment calls at the top, and the speaker is explicitly working to automate even that
data.name: Humans compress to intent; a layered agent stack absorbs implementation

data.brief: The two unglamorous details in the enrich-note skill — a fixed tag vocabulary and a per-note enrichment timestamp — are what let a prompt become a nightly job. The timestamp makes reruns cheap and safe by scoping work to unprocessed items; the fixed vocabulary keeps repeated passes from drifting into an ever-growing taxonomy. Any agent skill intended to run unattended and repeatedly needs both properties, and most published skills have neither, which is why they demo well and degrade under schedule
data.name: Idempotence makes skills schedulable

data.brief: Only per-agent identity makes the full lifecycle work: audit logs (which agent did what, for which user, via which host), the ability to revoke/fire a misbehaving agent, and enterprise policy (per-user or per-host) — none possible when the agent hides behind the user, where the only recourse is disconnecting everything
data.name: Per-agent identity is what makes audit, revocation, and policy possible

data.brief: When one-shotting software approaches free, the scarce input inverts from engineering capacity to imagination — the valuable skill becomes stretching what you think is possible (PG's "live in the future, then build what's missing" as an operating prompt); design converges on taste-expression via sliders and generated variation rather than hand-built artifacts
data.name: When one-shotting software approaches free, the scarce input is imagination

data.brief: The metric that matters for local AI is impact per parameter, not parameter count: an open-frontier gap will always exist, but the densing curve shrinks it on a fixed cadence, so any capability seen in the cloud today is a countdown to running it on hardware you own — plan against the curve, not the current snapshot
data.name: The metric that matters for local AI is impact per parameter

data.brief: Agent self-disagreement usually isn't a model problem — the agent is surfacing ambiguity that already exists (underspecified labeling policy, missing disambiguating information) at the decision boundary where humans and classical classifiers also fail. Model disagreement is a feature, not a bug: each flip-flop is a pointer to exactly where clarification teaches the system the most
data.name: Agent self-disagreement surfaces existing ambiguity, not model failure

data.brief: The reason continual learning cannot be evaluated with existing benchmarks is not an oversight but a design commitment: instance independence was deliberately engineered into evaluation to make scores clean, comparable and unconfounded. That choice, sensible for measuring capability, structurally forbids measuring accumulation — and since the field optimizes what it measures, an entire dimension of progress has been invisible by construction. Fixing it requires building environments with shared latent structure and drift, which is expensive in exactly the way independent benchmarks were designed to avoid
data.name: Independence was designed in

data.brief: The AI infra market re-writes its rules every 3–6 months and every vendor's pitch matches its position (Jensen Huang: token factories; Satya Nadella: unmetered local intelligence; neoclouds: endpoint providers capture the value) — so builders must derive the rent-vs-own answer from their own workload, not the marketplace narrative
data.name: Infra market rewrites its rules every 3-6 months; judge rent-vs-own by workload

data.brief: Agents can run the inner execution loop (investigate, implement, test, report); the outer loop — decide, verify, approve, own — is still engineering. The boundary is not "human looks at AI output"; it is evidence and responsibility. Inner loop is capability, outer loop is agency
data.name: Inner loop is capability, outer loop — decide, verify, approve, own — is agency

data.brief: The first three layers (identity, conditions, voice) are instructions — probabilistic requests to a system that usually complies; the fourth reads what actually came out and decides whether it may leave the business. Instructions are prompt engineering (asking nicely and hoping); permission is systems engineering (checking and being sure). One mechanism cannot simultaneously be inviolable, situational, expressive, and self-checking — pull the jobs apart and give each a layer built for it, and "turn 21" stops breaking
data.name: Instructions are prompt engineering; permission is systems engineering

data.brief: Human-in-the-loop is a cycle, not a line: model → interaction → human behavior → data → next model. The interface determines which labels get logged — rubber-stamp UIs breed a vicious cycle (confident model, deferent human, false positives logged as truth), while structured, friction-matched interactions surface honest disagreement that compounds into targeted model improvement
data.name: The interface determines which labels get logged in the human-AI cycle

data.brief: The interface is rented, the verification loop is owned: a REPL wins today only because coding is what current models are best at (computer use may take over); the domain engines behind the feedback loop appreciate with every model release
data.name: The interface is rented; the verification loop is owned

data.brief: The compounding investments are a personal memory system and team plugins: like an employee of seven years, an agent with long history + pinned threads + memory needs only a high-level ask; the "AI champion" who builds team plugins becomes a company-wide force multiplier
data.name: The compounding investments are personal memory and team plugins

data.brief: Model-judged code quality is self-limiting: a model that could reliably recognize good code would already write it; so quality verification cannot be fully delegated back to the same class of model being verified
data.name: Model-judged code quality is self-limiting

data.brief: With non-deterministic systems the tempting move — hyperfixating on one failing run and patching the prompt from its trace — is the trap. The unit of judgment is the failure *pattern*: the golden set needs multiple examples covering each pattern, and the question is how often the system fails on that pattern, not whether it failed on that example. Traces are for understanding *why* a pattern exists, not for deciding whether a change is warranted.
data.name: The unit of judgment is the failure pattern, not the individual run

data.brief: Ship the kill switch before anything else: one agent-wide plus one per-tool toggle, effective in seconds without deployment, changes operational posture more than any other engineering investment in the quarter — the four cited incidents all become 30-second mitigations with one
data.name: Ship the kill switch before anything else

data.brief: Agent knowledge splits into three kinds with a historical arc: intrinsic (parametric — what powered the Copilot/ChatGPT inflection and the '96-IntelliSense-to-zero-handwritten-code exponential), extrinsic (RAG grown into context engineering and company-wide grounding), and learned (loops that observe agents doing the work and tune them from traces). The learned kind is the newest leg and the one that captures what's unique to each organization — its differentiation
data.name: Agent knowledge splits into intrinsic, extrinsic, and learned kinds

data.brief: When a customer adopts your vocabulary, they adopt your model of their own business — so the durable position is not the feature set but the noun-and-verb layer everything else is expressed in. Definitional ambiguity is a feature of how humans work in their own domains, not a bug to be schematized away; the winning move is to canonicalize it inside the platform so every later question, integration and tool is phrased in your terms. The corollary for AI vendors is immediate: whoever fixes what skill, MCP and agent mean occupies the same position Palantir's ontology did.
data.name: The durable position is the noun-and-verb layer, not the feature set

data.brief: Sub-second retrieval is not an optimization but a capability threshold: below it you have a batch pipeline, above it you have something an agent can call mid-reasoning, so latency decides which products can exist at all. And it's won by scoping and accumulation of small cuts, not breakthroughs — which means the agent-data layer competes on operational engineering, the same conclusion the CUA-infrastructure talks reach from the browser side. The 400M→6B request jump shows the reward: crossing the latency gate unlocks a different order of demand
data.name: Latency is a capability gate

data.brief: Real-time model selection is about serving characteristics, not intelligence or parameter count — a "small" model on a throughput-oriented platform can be 10x too slow while a Haiku-class model on a latency-prioritized platform meets budget; capability moved out of the bottleneck, the inference layer moved in
data.name: Real-time model selection is about serving characteristics, not IQ

data.brief: Every time writing software got cheaper (high-level languages, frameworks, cloud, low-code) demand expanded rather than shrank; agents repeat the pattern — the bottleneck moves from "can we build this" to "should this exist and can we answer for it"
data.name: Cheaper software expands demand; the bottleneck moves to should this exist

data.brief: Most AI-engineering bugs come from computation living on the wrong side of one boundary: latent space (the LLM — taste, judgment, decoding vague human intent, steered by markdown) vs deterministic space (code — state, storage, exact computation). His example: seating 800 people optimally at Startup School must keep the seat-assignment array out of the context window; the LLM does the human-judgment part. Getting placement right turns a month of work into ~10 minutes and a few hundred dollars of tokens
data.name: Most AI-engineering bugs come from computation on the wrong side of one boundary

data.brief: A knowledge platform must layer its complexity: turnkey at the top ("here are my PDFs, deal with them" — chunking, vectorization, ranking under the covers) with expert control at the bottom (index structure, vector quantization, lexical retrieval) in the same stack, so teams move up and down as needs change; plus token-efficiency as a first-class retrieval metric (most information-dense answer in fewest tokens)
data.name: Knowledge platforms must layer turnkey tops over expert-control bottoms

data.brief: The durable claim is about *where* a production system should accumulate its corrections. In the weights, every correction is a week-long retrain with regression risk and freezes the model and the architecture around it; in the context (skills, resources, prompts, a curated validation set), a correction is an hour and the model stays swappable. That is pat-harness-over-model stated as a maintenance-economics result — and a caution for the continual-learning thesis: the accumulation loop that compounds is the one that lives *outside* the weights
data.name: Learning in weights calcifies learning in context flows

data.brief: The durable claim beneath the promotion: the trifecta is answered at the organizational layer — who an agent is, on whose authority, within what boundary — and that layer needs a public registrar and legal standing more than it needs a better model. Blockchains' role shrinks to the audit trail; the enabling act was a state statute. Whether kidunas succeed or not, "agent organizations with legal personhood" is now a thing that exists
data.name: Legal standing is the missing agent commerce primitive

data.brief: Duration is the wrong instrument. You can manufacture an arbitrarily "long-horizon" task by chaining unrelated independent subtasks and learn nothing about the model; what measures capability is state coupling (early decisions constraining later ones), tool-coordination breadth, and ambiguity at the start. Environment design, not task length, is the capability instrument — which is why benchmark comparisons on average-hours are close to meaningless without the complexity profile.
data.name: Duration is the wrong instrument; state coupling and ambiguity measure capability

data.brief: The talk's TLDR and its transferable lesson beyond security: don't define the task by a single known answer — let the artifact define the task. Attempts to author a perfect single-bug environment fail even with $60M and expert curation, and the model punishes the imperfection by reward-hacking the easiest path. The fix is not a better-curated environment but open-world grading: ask for everything, demand executable proof for each claim, deduplicate deterministically, and renormalize ground truth when the model finds something you did not know.
data.name: Let the artifact define the task, not a single known answer

data.brief: Deriving context is lossy and generative, so lineage cannot be reconstructed or logged after the fact — it must be engineered into the data structure itself, which is a graph keeping sources verbatim and linking everything derived back to them; compliance, veracity assessment, debugging ("why do I have this fact?"), and deletion decisions then fall out of the structure for free.
data.name: Lineage cannot be logged after the fact — it must be engineered into the structure

data.brief: The core design tension of agentic work systems: verification kills liveness (a human-reviewed task stops moving) and liveness kills verification (unapproved work compounds into slop that is worse than nothing); a naive for-loop over a task manager collapses once dependency trees, blockers, multi-agent handoffs, and checkout locks enter — the balance must be enforced by a control plane with contracts, not by the agents
data.name: Verification kills liveness and liveness kills verification

data.brief: LLM judges import bias: Claude Opus judging graded Llama's near-indistinguishable summaries harsher than sibling Claude Sonnet's ("angsty" vs "cross" quibbles) — eval scores can't be trusted until you open the raw comparisons; judge strictness/self-preference can masquerade as a capability gap
data.name: LLM judges import bias — judge strictness can masquerade as a capability gap

data.brief: Keep the LLM on what it's uniquely good at — parsing ambiguous requests, judging where/what to look for, handling never-seen phrasing, synthesizing the human-readable answer — and move everything data-modelable into code: retrieval, exact set logic, counting, dedup across near-identical names, anything that must be 100% reproducible. Structured outputs are the interface: the LLM emits the search plan, deterministic code executes it with perfect recall
data.name: Keep the LLM on judgment; move everything data-modelable into code

data.brief: Local AI is "in the '90s of the Linux operating system" (Osman): capability has arrived (frontier-class open weights on desk-side hardware) but infrastructure and UX haven't — adoption is gated on point-and-click onboarding ("as simple as opening Cursor"), not capability; the real trade-off to engineer is simplicity vs customizability, and the answer must live in software that figures itself out (ODS auto-selecting models per device), never in documentation; ChatGPT-grade users are lost the moment quantization becomes their homework
data.name: Local AI is in its Linux-90s moment: capability arrived, UX has not
