data.brief: Always-on agents changed both curves that matter: reasoning + agents burn tokens continuously (not per-question), so cloud cost scales with time instead of usage — local caps it flat; and usefulness now requires feeding agents the crown jewels (enterprise IP, health records, home-camera footage), which nobody wants leaving the building — local keeps everything "in the room." The two arguments arrive together, which is why the inflection is now rather than when local models first got good
data.name: Always-on agents make local AI answer both the cost and privacy curves

data.brief: The future of AI need not be one centralized brain; it can be billions of small local brains, each running on a personal device and shaped by the individual it serves — enabling privacy, offline capability, and deep personalization for gameplay
data.name: The future can be billions of small local brains, not one centralized brain

data.brief: Logging is the precondition of every loop above it, and its *shape* decides who can use it: one flat end-to-end record per run — rather than nested per-agent traces — lets engineers, PMs and non-technical staff all drill into a single case and roll the same fields up in aggregate. Start there, because without it there is nothing to optimize for, let alone a self-learning loop to build.
data.name: Flat end-to-end logging is the precondition for every loop above it

data.brief: Because the log records the agent's identity and everything it saw and did, log custody is the real sovereignty question of the managed-agents era: a provider hosting your loop, memory, and compaction under its policies, queryable by its systems, doesn't just host your agent — it owns it; the long-term valuable part is the log, since model, runtime, and machines are all replaceable
data.name: Log custody is the real sovereignty question of the managed-agents era

data.brief: "Long-horizon is not just an engineering problem, it is a mindset." The argument: humanity's real targets — cure cancer, the Millennium Prize problems, getting to Mars — are all measured in years, so an AI that matters has to be built for horizons it cannot see the end of, and that requires patience as a design stance rather than a longer context window. The industry has instead optimized for what fits inside a rollout: coding and procedural tasks phrased as "do this, fix that", with one or two admissible solutions and no room for creativity, evaluated in worlds with no other players in them.
data.description: KellyBench is the demonstration — put frontier models in a one-year, open-ended, adversarial, real-money task and all of them lose money. What we can measure cheaply is what we train on, and therefore what we stay bad at is exactly what we cannot cheaply measure.
data.name: Long-horizon is a mindset: we stay bad at exactly what we cannot cheaply measure

data.brief: Why "loops are the new thing" is deeper than fashion: Böhm–Jacopini (1966) proved sequence + conditional + iteration suffice for Turing completeness. Prompt-era LLM systems had sequences and some branching; the agentic loop supplies the third primitive — which is exactly why the field's figureheads describe their job as writing loops (Cherny; Steinberger: "I don't code anymore, I just design loops that prompt agents"). The excitement is the arrival of general computability in the LLM stack — and it is a property of the *harness structure*, not of the model inside it
data.name: Loop is the turing step

data.brief: The one point all four debaters converged on: a loop is only as good as the cheap deterministic verification wired around it — types, linters, pre-commit hooks, simulators, deterministic system tests. Loop engineering = preventing the loop from closing until it satisfies your certification ("the model's a drunk... we engineer away the failure domains"); adding non-deterministic verifiers instead compounds error
data.name: A loop is only as good as the cheap deterministic verification around it

data.brief: Loop engineering doesn't need new theory, it needs an old one. What separates a loop you can run on a real codebase from a blind one is whether you can name its set point, sensor, measured error, controller and actuator — and above all whether the controller exists and is tuned, because a loop with no controller makes too large a change or the wrong change and then repeats it.
data.description: The payoff is not only safety: an incremental, well-instrumented loop produces diffs small enough that humans keep reading the code, and a control signal carrying telemetry makes the loop improve the code it touches instead of transliterating it.
data.name: Loop engineering needs an old theory: the controller is the load-bearing part

data.brief: The unglamorous claim under all three war stories is that the defensible product in the agent-data layer is *maintenance*, not any artifact: scrapers break, layouts shift, anti-bot detection evolves, so "you build the intelligence, we take the messy maintenance" is the actual value exchange. That is why the layer is a subscription and why it resists disintermediation — the same reason Primor's owned-context compounds and Klein's infrastructure consistency matters. Three vendors in one track converge on "the web's constant change is the business"
data.name: Maintenance is the moat

data.brief: When in doubt, manage agents like other humans: the trust mechanisms we already run for people — commander's intent instead of micromanagement, onboarding guides/librarians, second opinions, juries of peers — port directly to agent design and beat both bleeding-edge optimizations and prompt incantations in day-to-day practice. All three of the talk's shipped examples are org-design patterns, not model tricks
data.name: When in doubt, manage agents like other humans

data.brief: Vetting is only enforceable if there is exactly one place skills come from. Making the internal marketplace canonical — publication by pull request, third-party downloads uploaded before use — is what converts an unenforceable policy into a CI step, and it doubles as the mechanism for safe sharing. The corollary is that the security property degrades the moment a second marketplace appears, which is why proactively detecting new marketplaces (and installing the scanner into them) is the named next problem.
data.name: One canonical marketplace is what makes skill vetting enforceable

data.brief: There is no one-size-fits-all retrieval: choose the architecture by corpus churn rate and relevance density — stable + deeply interconnected → GraphRAG; fast-replacement + all-documents-relevant → parallel CAG buckets; sparse relevance at scale → plain vector RAG; every strategy trades compute, cost, and speed differently, so fit the solution to the specific problem rather than defaulting to one stack
data.name: Choose retrieval architecture by corpus churn rate and relevance density

data.brief: The industry reads model competence as a property of models; it is better read as a property of domains. Code decomposes, executes and verifies — so code got solved. Everything that resists decomposition is still open, and will stay open until someone does the measurement engineering. That reframes the subjective frontier as a construction problem with a defined method: decompose the domain, find the components that are already codified somewhere (a brand book is a design domain that experts already decomposed and wrote down), make them observable, and route what remains.
data.description: It also predicts where progress will come from — not from a better base model, but from whoever can drag more of a fuzzy domain leftward into verifiability.
data.name: Model competence is a property of domains, not of models

data.brief: The talk's sharp point is that the interesting frontier in generative video has moved from model quality (already photorealistic) to serving efficiency and orchestration — cost-per-hour, steerability-under-a-second, and wiring multiple models into synchronized real-time streams. That mirrors the LLM story exactly: once the model is good enough, value migrates to the layers around it (inference, harness, agent access), which is why a media company positions itself as an inference provider and ships CLI/MCP for agents rather than a better model
data.name: Media frontier is serving not quality

data.brief: Asking an AI to use a canvas is like asking a human to handwrite SVG — capability verdicts are artifacts of the medium: "think like the model" (tokens, language, structure) rather than "think like a user" (pixels, coordinates), and abilities that benchmarks score as absent (spatial layout) appear, with the browser doing the geometry so the model never places a coordinate
data.name: Capability verdicts are artifacts of the medium: think like the model

data.brief: The two headline results form a decision rule that most memory adoption skips: below the context window, memory is pure overhead — same accuracy, higher cost — and above it, the *policy* rather than the machinery decides the outcome. Teams reaching for a memory system should first establish which regime they are in, because the honest answer for a large share of production tasks is that the task fits and the memory layer is buying nothing but tokens. That framing also explains why memory benchmarks disagree so violently: they are sampling different sides of the same threshold
data.name: Memory earns its keep only past the window

data.brief: The durable asset is a harness-agnostic memory layer of plain files + references sitting between whichever agent harness you use and your accumulated knowledge: harnesses are swappable (Claude Code, Codex), per-session context is disposable, but the wiki compounds — the answer to "why not just use Codex Cloud or NotebookLM" is that you are, and you still need the layer in between
data.name: The durable asset is a harness-agnostic memory layer of plain files

data.brief: The differentiating asset was never a smarter model — "the brain isn't a smarter model, it's a really well-organized memory." Off-the-shelf models reading structured private history (vectors + graph + corrections-win + salience gating) beat the fine-tuning reflex; "the expensive part was never compute, it was teaching a company to remember itself"
data.name: The brain isn't a smarter model, it's a really well-organized memory

data.brief: The surprising fact about the world's largest model host is that its database holds no models. Hosting weights is an object-storage problem and effectively solved; making 3M of them findable, listable, billable and access-controlled is a metadata problem, and that is where the engineering lives. Separating the two lets metadata, binaries and compute be scaled and tuned independently — and it means the platform's growth pressure shows up first as query latency and read distribution, not as storage cost.
data.name: The world's largest model host stores no models: metadata is the workload

data.brief: On mobile the client is effectively immutable: hundreds of millions of installs, no control over update timing, and an unknown content type doesn't degrade gracefully — it crashes for weeks. So trust must live server-side: fixed component menus the model can't extend, version-gated capability maps, and a BFF that absorbs model output so the client stays dumb and safe
data.name: On mobile the client is effectively immutable; trust must live server-side

data.brief: The model layer is unlikely to hold the value it is currently priced for. Historical frame: no pioneer of an infrastructure technology has held more than 10% of the market long-run — railroads built company towns and charged tyrannical rents right up until the automobile arrived and they were nationalized; AWS and Google consolidated the infrastructure layer and never captured the application layer.
data.description: OpenAI and Anthropic are carving fiefdoms with anti-distillation terms, export controls and enterprise exclusivity, and GLM 5.2 surpassing GPT on real-world rubrics is hard proof that app-layer companies can already decouple. But models differ on efficiency and modality, so they are not fungible like electricity: the endpoint is neither nationalization nor durable lock-in, and what to build next hinges on whether a general enterprise can decouple models from foundation-model labs.
data.name: The model layer is unlikely to hold the value it is priced for

data.brief: Never let the model directly control production systems: the model generates proposals; deterministic infrastructure validates them, a policy engine approves them, an execution gateway enforces them. Reliability becomes buildable on top of a probabilistic model precisely because the platform, not the model, holds authority
data.name: The model suggests, the platform decides

data.brief: Division of labor: the model is "the talent" (great at delivering a line) and the harness is "the director" (owns where you are in the process); ask the model only to execute one single-step contract at a time
data.name: The model is the talent, the harness is the director

data.brief: Indeterministic LLM extraction can't be blindly tested, so it only improves efficiency; corroborating an independent second/third source is what converts "efficiency gain" into genuine human elimination
data.name: Corroborating independent sources converts efficiency gains into human elimination

data.brief: Moving an agent from one user to a group changes the engineering problem, not its size. Three properties that are trivial or absent for a personal agent become the whole design: what gets in (a guard, against a surface that now includes everyone's messages and pastes), what is kept (memory that is curated, temporally weighted and continually re-scored, because a group's context evolves under you), and who hears the answer (channel, recipient and moment — DM vs group, glasses vs car speaker, and often silence). The privacy rule underneath is contextual, not classificatory: sensitivity is a property of the room, so permissions have to travel with the audience rather than with the datum.
data.name: Multi-user agents need a social layer: guard, memory and recipient routing

data.brief: Making AI use visible and multiplayer (public channels, shared sessions) creates social accountability that levels up how everyone uses the tool and suppresses slop — "you want to do work you're proud to do in public"; team norms transmit by observation rather than policy
data.name: Visible, multiplayer AI use creates social accountability that suppresses slop

data.brief: The industry is centering agents; the unsolved layer is the people around them. Individual agent leverage is real but strands work on laptops and in single-player chats — the compounding gains come from team infrastructure: one session addressable from every surface, visibility trails that answer "who vetted this," ambient ingestion that turns organizational exhaust (meetings, bug reports, support chatter) into evaluable code, and sandboxes safe enough that non-engineers trigger real work. The model was never the blocker for any of this; the coordination fabric was
data.name: Multiplayer is the unbuilt layer

data.brief: Teaching a model your DSL or custom JSON discards its pretraining ("asking Shakespeare to write a poem in Japanese" — examples don't fix a non-native tongue); adopting the model's native format instead turns the entire scraped web into your product's training corpus and every model upgrade into free product improvement — the format compounds with the frontier rather than fighting it
data.name: Adopting the model's native format compounds with the frontier

data.brief: The advice Bai gives everyone considering FDE: ask whether you need one, not whether you want one — it is easy to want what is in vogue. Two qualifying questions: do you have to sell something technically complicated to a non-technical buyer, and do you have (or will you invest in) a platform of shared primitives for FDEs to build on?
data.description: A "no" to either means DevRel or a sales-led motion instead; a "yes" to the first and "no" to the second guarantees a maintenance burden that outruns the revenue.
data.name: Ask whether you need an FDE function, not whether you want one

data.brief: There is no golden dataset that is good for everything: a dataset is only optimal with respect to a particular set of output tasks — a great legal model wants legal data more than healthcare data, and vice versa — which is why curation has to start from the target task distribution rather than from a quality score. Three properties define a good mix and they are in tension: relevance to the intended outputs, diversity (most model brittleness comes from insufficiently diverse training data — the model answers correctly when the question is posed just so, and breaks when it is posed slightly differently), and correct mixing and sequencing across sources and stages.
data.description: The practical rule that falls out: past a threshold, repeating high-quality data beats showing low-quality data.
data.name: There is no golden dataset: a mix is only optimal for a target task distribution

data.brief: Even the cleanest real-world target function leaks subjectivity: arXiv authors have creative freedom in choosing primary labels, capping the loop's accuracy near 80% — and any target given to an agent is always incomplete (the goal you specify is not quite the destination you want). Every domain therefore ultimately needs human/domain-expert calibration and periodic re-grounding, not a set-and-forget objective
data.name: Even the cleanest real-world target function leaks subjectivity

data.brief: In a fast-churning extension ecosystem, refusing to adopt is information, not lag: the agent clients that skipped experimental MCP Tasks V1 dodged a stateful protocol that is being discarded within a year, while any early implementer would now be rewriting. When the spec surface itself is unstable, adoption timing is a risk decision — and the vendor most invested in the capability is the one telling you the holdouts were right
data.name: Non adoption as competence

data.brief: The same runtime LLMs that make every play session unique dissolve the known-codebase stability contract; a platform expecting millions of pieces of AI-created gaming content must re-solve verification from scratch — debugging non-deterministic stacks, content safety for content generated at runtime, and a token economy that keeps creators, players, and platform simultaneously profitable
data.name: Runtime uniqueness dissolves the stability contract; verification must be re-solved

data.brief: S3-as-source-of-truth with hot caches is doing to AI-era data what commodity cloud did to compute: a ~100× price collapse turned retrieval from a killed feature into a default layer, an 8-person Cursor bet its business on it, and the same shape is queued up for KV caches and beyond. The durable insight is architectural, not product-specific: design storage to object-store durability + P99 round-trip math, and the workloads that "couldn't line up" economically start lining up
data.name: Object storage is the ai storage endgame

data.brief: Eras in AI are set by what the objective optimizes for, not by how capable the models are. RLHF optimizes human preference and produced the assistance era — chat, copilots, coding agents, everything with a person waiting at the end of the loop. RLVR optimizes pure correctness and produced the verifiable-domain wins. Neither optimizes for making a calibrated decision nobody will check, which is why automation is still "a rounding error despite LLMs' intelligence" while benchmark scores keep falling. Read this way the field's disagreement dissolves: the optimists are measuring the objective we trained for, the pessimists are measuring the one we didn't.
data.name: Eras in AI are set by what the objective optimizes for, not by model capability

data.brief: The transferable lesson is that at multi-node scale the binding constraint is the interconnect, not the accelerator, and the default dashboards hide exactly that — GPU-utilization flatters, while the InfiniBand/NVLink metrics that actually predict failure are unexported and must be built. Any team scaling past a single node that trusts the vendor's default utilization number is flying blind on the thing most likely to kill its runs, which is why "metrics are everything" is the first lesson rather than an afterthought
data.name: Observe the fabric not the gpu

data.brief: The unit of enterprise delivery is inverting: not a bespoke agent per domain, but one good general-purpose coding agent (~10 tools) as the engine, with domain skills layered on top — switching industries becomes writing skills, not building agents
data.name: Unit of delivery inverts: one general agent plus domain skills

data.brief: Persisting every agent event to a durable log is a single decision that pays out three times — observability for humans, context recovery for the model, and a training substrate for memory and dreaming — which is why several independent teams keep converging on it from different motivations. The non-obvious part is the second: decoupling the session record from the context window means discarded context is retrievable, converting compaction from a lossy one-way operation into a reversible view over a complete record. Any harness that treats the context window as the session has foreclosed both the recovery and the self-improvement capability without realizing it
data.name: One log three capabilities

data.brief: Per the 1/9/90 rule, transformation fails if it depends on every engineer leveling up; invest a handpicked 1% (champions) in the shared substrate — the repos — so agents work well for everyone, then delegation surfaces where work already arrives make agent use native for the other 99%
data.name: Invest a handpicked 1% in the shared substrate so agents work for everyone

data.brief: A ~1:1 researcher-to-microservice ratio in a decoupled monorepo lets each research initiative grow and iterate independently behind a gateway while still conforming to production practice (layered architecture, type contracts, CI, containerization) — researcher velocity and production discipline stop trading off
data.name: A ~1:1 researcher-to-microservice ratio ends the velocity-discipline trade-off

data.brief: Cloud infra and foundation models are commoditizing. What stays proprietary — data, policies, workflows, ontology — is now the moat. Local frontier models + agent-driven setup collapse on-prem cost; sovereign AI flips from escape hatch to default.
data.description: For two decades, cloud was the default and on-prem was the compliance escape hatch. That relationship is inverting. Open-source frontier models (Kimi K2.5's 1T/32B MoE at 76% lower cost under Modified MIT) are deployable on commodity hardware. Agents now configure firmware, networking, Kubernetes, and Terraform in hours — collapsing the operational tax that made self-hosting impractical. Turnkey platforms (Zylon: air-gapped in under a week) productize the playbook. What remains — and becomes the durable moat — is the stack each company owns: their data, their policies, their workflows, their ontology. Cloud infrastructure and foundation models commoditize fast; the moat moves inward. 'On-prem is the new cloud' isn't hardware nostalgia — it's the recognition that sovereign data and sovereign reasoning are the new platform advantage.
data.importance: Inverts the 20-year default. As cloud and foundation models commoditize, the durable moat moves inward — to the data, ontology, and workflows each company owns.
data.name: On-prem is the new cloud

data.brief: Working definitions that cut through the summer's buzzword fog: an ontology helps something interpret and reason about the data; a semantic layer establishes the consistent agreed-upon terms so the data can be queried accurately. Different jobs, both graph-representable.
data.name: Ontology aids interpretation; semantic layer fixes agreed terms — different jobs

data.brief: OpenAI is running an open-ecosystem flywheel around a closed model: give away the harness, app server, plugins, and file conventions; use the identical stack internally; bake agent needs (compaction) into the public API first; feed the open harness into post-training. Every external fork and edge-case found returns as model and product improvement — the harness layer is where the ecosystem competes, while the model stays the swappable center
data.name: OpenAI runs an open-ecosystem flywheel around a closed model

data.brief: Open/self-hosted LLMs are re-running the Linux playbook, and the coexistence is structural, not transitional. Closed frontier ≈ the Mac/ChatGPT tier — accessible, individually optimal, $20/month; open models ≈ the Linux layer that ends up running enterprises, clouds, hyperscalers and neoclouds (Fireworks, Together, Baseten), because hyper-optimization "is not possible behind closed doors — you're shutting too many people out of the room" and resource-constrained contributors are who optimize a stack hardest. Both grow; the headline-friendly either/or never arrives
data.name: Open models are the linux layer

data.brief: AI split the meaning of "open source" in two, and the halves are moving in opposite directions. The community half — contribution, review, trust-building between strangers — is dying, because free generation destroyed the economics of verifying strangers' work (slop PRs, bug-report DDoS, contribution lockdowns). The artifact half — things freely usable and buildable-upon in public — is becoming more economically important than it has ever been, because open weights are the substrate the industry can standardize and commoditize on (the Open Compute mechanism). "Open source is dead; long live open source" is a precise claim: the social institution failed while the licensing institution ascends
data.name: Open source bifurcates

data.brief: Open weights are not a give-away but a loop with two suppliers: the lab ships the model and the architecture details early; the serving company writes the kernels, closes the quality gap at day zero and keeps compounding speedups afterwards; usage and PRs come back to the lab. Neither side can deliver "abundant intelligence" alone — the lab cannot serve at scale, the serving provider cannot train, and each new open model's distinct attention/MoE/quantization choices force the partnership to start early rather than at launch.
data.name: Open weights are a two-sided loop between the lab and the serving provider

data.brief: Log triage is a reasoning task (real bug vs. noise, symptom vs. root cause, deep-diving a fresh trajectory), so the ops layer must itself be agents — and they only work when given everything a human debugger gets: trajectories, metrics, database, UI, and code (e.g. the computer-use agent must be able to check the DB and trajectories to chase what it finds). Anything less produces guesses, not grounded diagnoses
data.name: Ops agents only work when given human-grade access to the system

data.brief: The harness-then-finetune ordering is really a rule about feedback latency: prefer whatever closes the loop fastest, because iteration count dominates per-iteration quality until you hit a ceiling. That explains why most teams stop at harness engineering and are right to — two-minute feedback beats a training run for almost every problem — and it reframes fine-tuning not as the mature endpoint but as the thing you do specifically when your ceiling is provably reached and your task distribution is narrow enough that a small model can be pushed past a frontier one on it
data.name: Optimize for feedback latency

data.brief: Model optionality is the negotiating leverage: oligopoly pricing follows gas-station dynamics (the #2 model only needs to be $1/M-tokens cheaper), so price does not correlate with capability, leaders rotate monthly, and a lab-exclusive discount that removes your ability to walk is the most expensive decision you can make — worse than the engineering cost of interoperability.
data.name: Model optionality is the negotiating leverage against oligopoly pricing

data.brief: Oracle-vs-actual deltas prove model capability is already sufficient for deep knowledge work — the recoverable gap lives in the search tool and harness (tool separation by intent, context budgeting via summaries/dedup, query framing), so closing it is retrieval engineering, not bigger models
data.name: Oracle-vs-actual deltas prove the recoverable gap lives in search tooling

data.brief: Read as history, the graph era was control borrowed from the harness while models were weak and returned to the model when they weren't — the same ladder Box's CTO described (b22) — which means "harness over model" is a moving boundary whose position must be re-measured with each model generation, exactly as the evals must. The counter-edge is recorded on purpose: the corpus's harness thesis should carry its own date stamp
data.name: Orchestration graphs were borrowed control

data.brief: Users never see queues, locks or commit paths — they see behaviour, and they read ordering bugs as personality: a lost correction feels forgetful, a stuck lane feels dead, completion-before-delivery feels confused. Concurrency control in an agent is therefore not an internal implementation detail but a user-facing product property.
data.name: Ordering is a product feature: users read concurrency bugs as personality

data.brief: Every organizational primitive maps onto harness constructs: a skill file is an employee (one capability, written clearly enough to execute), a resolver table is the org chart (routes each task to who handles it), filing rules are internal process, trigger evals are performance reviews. Companies were always "organizations of written procedure" — what was missing was a management layer for executing them, and that's what a harness is: sitting down with Claude Code/Codex is hiring, training, and managing a workforce made of markdown
data.name: Every organizational primitive maps onto harness constructs

data.brief: Once scanning industrializes (solvable with compute and money), the real bottlenecks are organizational: vulnerability routing at 100s/month, severity calibration between product and security engineers, and patch-review bandwidth — "non-technical problems are an order of magnitude harder than technical problems"; threat models stuck in people's heads are the scarcest input
data.name: Once scanning industrializes, the real bottlenecks are organizational

data.brief: Once agent memory is org-scoped rather than per-developer, the agent's usable context exceeds any individual's: prior sessions become retrievable precedent, best practices propagate by replaying respected engineers' work, and consistency emerges as a side effect — a company-brain effect assembled from work artifacts (repos + sessions) rather than from documents
data.name: Org-scoped agent memory exceeds any individual's usable context

data.brief: If intelligence and expertise are genuinely orthogonal axes rather than points on one curve, then the industry's central question stops being "how much smarter can the model get" and becomes "how steep can the accumulation slope be." That reframing is what makes the whole continual-learning track commercially coherent: it locates a source of compounding advantage that is not buying more pre-training compute, and it explains why the same frontier model can be transformative in one company and useless in another — the model is the intercept, the learning loop is the slope
data.name: Orthogonality changes the scaling question

data.brief: "Capabilities overhang" is doing precise work in this talk: it names the gap between what models can already do and what deployed systems extract, and locates the profit in closing it with engineering rather than waiting. That framing explains the whole batch's vendor lineup — harness sellers, infrastructure sellers, identity brokers all monetize the same overhang — and it makes a testable prediction: if the overhang is real, CUA deployment should inflect *without* a frontier-model release, purely on tooling. The half-empty room is the market mispricing that bet
data.name: Overhang is a vendor opportunity map

data.brief: In a care setting, false positives are not the conservative default — they are a distinct class of harm. Refusing someone at their lowest point isolates them and can prevent them from getting care, which means precision of intervention is itself a safety property, not a UX nicety.
data.description: That reframing has an organisational consequence: the accountable definition of correct cannot come from the engineering team's judgment or from the model provider's global calibration, it has to come from the licensed professional who owns the clinical outcome — safety is helping to define the capability.
data.name: In care settings over-triggering is its own class of harm

data.brief: Agent frameworks are fine to start, but a production team with evolving use cases gets more from owning a thin agent loop built on strong general-purpose infrastructure (typed effects, structured concurrency, DI, out-of-the-box tracing) than from framework abstractions — the loop itself is small; the surrounding engineering is what scales, and full control of the loop is what "unlocks the full capabilities of the model" (paraphrase)
data.name: Own a thin agent loop built on strong general-purpose infrastructure

data.brief: At the current "find out" stage of agent tooling, practitioners prefer owning a composable terminal workflow (tmux + vibe-coded glue: lazygit, critique, port-killers) over polished vertical apps (Conductor, Happy) that lock them to one agent or someone else's relay — the durable asset is the workflow, and mobile access should wrap it, not replace it
data.name: Practitioners prefer owning a composable terminal workflow over vertical apps

data.brief: A private benchmark on your own codebase converts model churn from a loyalty problem into an empirical one: when the frontier shifts — or a frontier model is withdrawn days after arriving — switching is a data-backed default change, not a workflow migration. Agnosticism plus owned measurement is what keeps a team "at the right part of the frontier of cost, speed, quality" without being captured by any token seller, and it is the only credible substrate for per-task routing, since no third party knows what works on your repo
data.name: Owned benchmarks buy agility

data.brief: Owned GPUs appreciate in capability as models densify: the same 8× RTX 3090s that barely loaded Llama 2 70B can now run ~15 parallel agents on Qwen 3.5 27B, and 2020-era Ampere 3090s still sell above MSRP; meanwhile subsidized cloud tokens will lose their subsidies and gain restrictions — so the rent-vs-own question ("why fund someone else's data center?") tilts toward owning, for consumers and enterprises alike; open-source AI also needs enterprise owners to sustain the incentive loop for open-weight releases and licenses
data.name: Owned GPUs appreciate in capability as models densify

data.brief: Every institution humans built — checklists, org charts, filing cabinets — is a prosthetic for the 7±2-item working memory; agents hold ~1M tokens ("three Harry Potter books open at once"), yet a company is a library, not three books, so the librarian deciding which three books open per task (context engineering) determines whether agents are geniuses or goldfish. Model quality is rented; a curated brain is owned and compounds — "retrieval is easy; being worth retrieving from is the product." Tan's greenfield call: every company on earth is about to need a brain; the memory layer should be open the way Linux is open
data.name: Model quality is rented; a curated brain is owned and compounds

data.brief: The operator model's second dividend: owning the work means owning ground-truth traces of tasks that are not on the internet, which turns enablement (people using the agent) directly into evals, regression suites and post-training data. The accumulation loop the corpus keeps describing is, here, a property of the business structure rather than of the model
data.name: Owning the work owns the data

data.brief: In voice you cannot average latency — one slow P95 response kills the whole conversation, so tail latency and multi-turn instruction-following decay matter more than headline P50 benchmarks
data.name: In voice you cannot average latency; the P95 tail kills conversations

data.brief: At platform scale the tail is the product: 1% of 14M users is 140,000 people, so P99 matters more than P50, and a slow search bar simply sends developers elsewhere. The generalizable move is to shift work from query time to write time and from the primary to everywhere else — precompute tokens on insert, keep a denormalized read-only copy, refresh ranking on a 5-minute cadence, and route anything that can tolerate staleness away from the one node that cannot be replicated around. The user-facing goal is invisibility: "you never have to think about it… keeping the user experience simple no matter how complex it gets under the hood".
data.name: At platform scale the P99 tail is the product

data.brief: Document-parsing quality is upstream of every downstream AI property — RAG correctness, agent extraction/validation, fine-tuning data, even the future scientific record (the citation cascade shows one bad extraction compounding through papers that train tomorrow's models); engineering spend belongs there before model upgrades, because no model choice repairs garbled ingestion
data.name: Document-parsing quality is upstream of every downstream AI property

data.brief: This talk holds two claims the rest of the batch splits on: the model needs *more* (perception the coding agent lacks) and the harness needs *less* over time (it thins as the model improves). Reconciled, they say capability migrates into the model on the perception axis while the harness's job is temporary risk-containment during that migration — guardrails, handoff, audit — not permanent capability. That is the cleanest in-corpus statement of the harness-as-depreciating-scaffold view, from a team with visibility into both sides of the loop
data.name: Perception and harness move in opposite directions

data.brief: For browser agents the binding constraint is perception, not intelligence: a compressed full-page text view at ~1/10th the DOM's token cost beats frontier-model screenshot loops on speed, cost, and completion — upgrading the model cannot fix what its representation hides (a screenshot shows one viewport; the DOM drowns the signal). "Better eyes" beat "better brains"
data.name: For browser agents perception, not intelligence, is the binding constraint

data.brief: Across grounding, prompting, fine-tuning and scoring, the same result keeps appearing: the model already contains the persona, and every technique that works is a way of getting it out in a format the model wasn't trained to produce — or of preventing it from filling in a gap you left. Fine-tuning on some populations improves unseen ones because it teaches the survey task, not the groups; asking for free text and mapping it onto a scale beats asking for the scale directly; grounding works by removing the model's licence to invent.
data.description: And the corollary that stops this from being a "more context is better" story: richer persona construction amplified model bias in at least one study, moving reconstructions further from reality as detail increased — so the discipline is calibration against ground truth, not elaboration.
data.name: Persona work is elicitation engineering, and more detail can amplify bias

data.brief: "It's not your model, not your team, not your funding — it's you": as AI amplification compounds through 2026→2030, the founder's personal brand is the moat — AI can amplify your signal but cannot replace your authenticity; people want to buy from a real human, which is why founder-led sales remains the main early-stage motion and why it cannot be delegated
data.name: The founder's personal brand is the moat AI can amplify but not replace

data.brief: The unit of software inverts: from one blessed multi-tenant deployment serving all users to per-user instantiated code — gadget as document, blueprint as code-minus-data template, one Durable Object per instance. That single inversion dissolves both incumbent distribution regimes at once: the app-store gatekeeping model (nothing to review or sign when every instance is confined by construction) and the SaaS roadmap model (no feature backlog when each user's agent forks the app locally). The infrastructure precondition is the part incumbents lack: isolation cheap enough to give every user, per app, their own sandboxed client and server
data.name: Personal software inverts distribution

data.brief: The durable claim is where the difficulty moved: once a small open model can write on-brand copy and place blocks, per-user page generation is gated by inference latency (the 1–2 s conversion budget) and by grounding (RAG over the site, blocks not sites), not by model quality — so the engineering is continuous per-site evaluation of provider speed and a harness that boxes the generation. Personalization, the oldest unsolved promise in marketing, becomes an infrastructure and evaluation problem
data.name: Personalization became a latency problem

data.brief: The whole field is better understood through weather forecasting than through polling. Both were unlocked by compute plus data; both are accurate only inside a regime and degrade predictably past it; both are trustworthy exactly to the degree they've been validated against what actually happened. Adopting that frame changes the methodology outright: you validate like a forecaster (compare distributions against what humans actually said, estimate the noise in your ground truth) rather than like a pollster (add samples until it's significant), and you accept that re-running the model improves your estimate of the model, never the accuracy of the forecast.
data.description: It also sets a ceiling nobody can engineer past — the humans being modelled are only ~80% consistent with themselves two weeks later, so "83% aligned" is a number about a noisy target, not about a solved problem.
data.name: Synthetic personas are forecasts, so validate like a forecaster not a pollster

data.brief: The entire CI/packaging/registry/app-store stack exists to move a frozen artifact from build machine to run machine safely, reproducibly, once. The pipeline isn't failing — the constraint it was built for (software expensive to produce, cheap to run) went away. The next 20 years are about shipping the right version to anyone, with isolation and provenance making that safe instead of terrifying
data.name: The pipeline isn't failing; the constraint it was built for went away

data.brief: The talk's durable move is to relocate scarcity: when implementation is gradable it converges for free, so the scarce input is the un-gradable decision of what to point the machine at — and that decision is only defensible when it comes from proximity (a real domain, a relationship the model can't see, a bet on what hasn't happened). This reframes pat-value-of-judgement more precisely than "taste": broad taste is trainable, *situated* judgement is not
data.name: Pointing is the scarce input

data.brief: Evaluate policy before the credential exists: a denied request means the token was never minted — nothing to leak, replay, or steal. This inverts the detect-and-revoke posture of API-key security
data.name: Evaluate policy before the credential exists

data.brief: The load-bearing move is choosing *which representation* to synchronize. Nothing about the optimizer changed — the master weights and the FP32 update stay dense — but by defining the synchronized object as the low-precision view the rollout engine actually serves, an intractable 500 GB transfer becomes a 500 MB patch, and the argument gets *stronger* as serving precision drops toward FP8 and NVFP4. It is a reminder that in systems built from stacked numeric representations, the cheapest available abstraction boundary is often the one the hardware already rounds to, and that "bitwise equivalent" is what makes a delta safe to apply repeatedly where "approximately equal" would drift
data.name: Precision view is the sync boundary

data.brief: Ambiguity and staleness have engineering answers (hierarchy, lifecycle); preference does not — routing an agent to the right metric based on who is asking amounts to building a "hive mind" per team/individual and is the open research frontier of enterprise agents
data.name: Preference routing is the open research frontier of enterprise agents

data.brief: In RAG systems the ingestion layer — conversion to structured markdown plus a chunking strategy matched to each document's shape — determines answer quality, cost, and debuggability more than model choice does; vet the data before the LLM and the smallest model suffices, skip it and no model saves you
data.name: In RAG the ingestion layer determines quality more than model choice

data.brief: Research advantage compounds through access, not only through talent. The same idea — put RL pressure on the tokens between the thinking tags — was tried at Meta on Llama 2 base models with a 4,000-token context and produced state-of-the-art math with none of the reflective behaviour; tried two years later on better base models with more RL compute and bigger context windows, it produced o1 and R1. "The fact that OpenAI had a GPT-4-level model before anyone else allowed them to see further." The uncomfortable structural claim inside the anecdote: in an age of scaling, having the prerequisites does not merely make your experiments cheaper, it makes you smarter — you see ideas that are
data.description: invisible from a lower rung, which means research ideas are not independent of who can afford to test them.
data.name: Research advantage compounds through access: prerequisites let you see further

data.brief: A product's pricing model caps its harness intelligence: AI bundled into existing subscription margins structurally can't afford reasoning models, so trustworthiness is decided at tool-selection time — pick by tier attributes (model power, subagents, plan mode, MCP, file editing), not by the convenience of a subscription you already pay for
data.name: A product's pricing model caps its harness intelligence

data.brief: Read alongside the OPSD talk earlier in the same track, this file completes a shift in what distillation *is*: not compression of a larger model into a smaller one, but a general mechanism for converting privileged information into policy. Once that is the frame, the design questions become where privilege comes from, how much of it the student could plausibly have derived, and where in a trajectory to apply it — which is why both talks independently identify hint construction as the discipline that reward design was for RL. The 15%→80% online-versus-offline gap is the cleanest available evidence that *provenance* of the hint, not its content, carries the learning
data.name: Privileged information is the real axis

data.brief: The move that makes self-distillation work is recognizing that a teacher's only necessary property is being *better on this instance*, not being a bigger model — so privileged information substitutes for capability. That is what lets the technique survive at the frontier, where no larger teacher exists, and it reframes distillation from a compression technique into a general mechanism for converting hindsight into policy. It also explains the failure mode exactly: if the privilege cannot be earned by reasoning, the student learns to fake having earned it, which is why hint design becomes the discipline that reward design was for RL
data.name: Privileged information replaces the teacher

data.brief: Production agent memory is a different product from personalization memory: what matters is outcome-weighted reasoning — what to check before acting, which trajectories worked — not who the user is; systems built to remember preferences structurally cannot make an agent better at its job
data.name: Production agent memory is outcome-weighted reasoning, not personalization

data.brief: An embedded delivery motion only scales if the field is a funnel into the product, not a queue of bespoke work: every manual FDE action is a defect, repeats are the signal (25 hand-built CRM integrations produce the integration builder), and the destination is configuration in natural language by the customer or the agent-building team. Measured this way, the health of an FDE org is the rate at which custom becomes self-serve — and the compounding runs in both directions, since knowledge shared across deployments improves the agent for customer B every time it meets customer A.
data.name: An embedded delivery motion only scales if the field is a funnel into the product

data.brief: A benchmark measures the model plus its prompt and harness, and the prompt's effect is large enough to erase a capability: one line saying tests are handled suppresses self-verification in the strongest models available.
data.description: It follows that harness and template must be reported as part of a score — hence the agent-agnostic mini-SWE-agent for base-model comparison, the native-harness control runs, and the speaker's call for a class of benchmarks that measures harnesses rather than models.
data.name: A benchmark measures the model plus its prompt and harness

data.brief: Prompting is the punch-card protocol surviving into the AI era: package a complete turn, submit, wait, read, repair, resubmit — "batch with interactive sprinkles". Shrinking the wait from overnight to seconds fooled us into calling it interactive; "prompt engineering" is a flattering name for deck-assembly rules (think step-by-step, paste more/less context, markdown incantations). Model capacity curves up while the protocol stays flat — the human still chooses context, timing, notices ambiguity, repairs output — and when it fails, users wrongly blame themselves. The mismatch is the interface, not the user
data.name: Prompting is the punch-card batch protocol surviving into the AI era

data.brief: The durable claim: as agents act among strangers, the missing piece is not the rail but portable, selectively disclosed proof that a human authorized this scope, now — platforms can substitute logs and borrowed trust only inside closed ecosystems. Payments force the primitive first; every hard-to-reverse agent action will inherit it
data.name: Proof of authorization is the scarce primitive

data.brief: The speaker's stated takeaway: protect the whole developer AI workflow, not only the code it generates. Application-security programmes are aimed at generated artefacts, but the steering layer — skills, plugins, MCP servers, rules, hooks — is natural language, ships as configuration, carries higher default privilege than a code package, and is invisible to code scanners. Whoever authors that layer is writing code on other people's machines, so it needs the review discipline a dependency gets.
data.name: Protect the whole developer AI workflow, not only the code it generates

data.brief: The MCP/WebMCP debate keeps being argued as a technology question when the binding constraint is institutional: an API exists only where an organization can and will maintain one, and the long tail of the web is precisely the set of organizations that cannot. That makes protocol coverage a function of institutional capacity, not spec quality — and means the addressable-by-protocol web is permanently the head of the distribution. Any agent strategy that assumes protocol reach beyond it inherits the delusion, however good the spec
data.name: Protocol adoption is gated by institutions

data.brief: An LSP moment for agents: once agents speak a shared protocol they become swappable backends, and clients compete on rendering and capabilities — integration value accrues at the protocol layer, not in whose model powers the loop
data.name: An LSP moment for agents: shared protocol makes agents swappable backends

data.brief: Frontier models' production-displacing role: use the biggest model to prove feasibility and to mint the golden dataset, then let evals — not vibes or peer folklore ("everyone said Gemma 4 is best"; it ran ~8 s vs Llama's ~1 s here and lost) — pick the smallest model that passes: the "SAGE model" (smallest-and-good-enough, her coinage)
data.name: Prototype big, deploy small: evals pick the smallest model that passes

data.brief: When capture is ambient and total, the threat model must include the operator itself — inside a bigtech acquirer that gets harder, not easier (customer-facing guarantees stop applying to you). Trust then can't be policy — it must be verifiable architecture: public transparency logs, attestation, org-split signing keys, and a TCB small enough (~20k LOC) for outside auditors to actually verify
data.name: Ambient capture makes the operator the threat model; trust must be verifiable architecture

data.brief: Self-hosted agents are only safely useful when you can expose them: gating the control plane (and anything the agent serves, like MCP endpoints) behind an identity-aware proxy lets local agent workspaces be reached from ChatGPT, phones, and chat apps without tokens in query strings or device pairing — hardening and usability stop being a trade-off
data.name: Identity-aware proxies make self-hosted agents safely reachable

data.brief: Psychometrics offers a mostly untapped research program for LLMs: multidimensional/hierarchical models for per-skill ability, merging benchmarks under one scale (cf. the Meta-Benchmark paper), auxiliary signals (latency, tokens) as ability indicators, and psychometric measurement of alignment coupled to mechanistic interpretability
data.name: Psychometrics offers a mostly untapped research program for LLMs

data.brief: Public benchmark scores that people use to calibrate new model releases are inflated by reward hacking (git-history archaeology, online answer lookup) and don't test real-world conditions; private held-out evals built from your own codebase's real tasks are the trustworthy measure
data.name: Public benchmark scores are inflated; private held-out evals are the trustworthy measure

data.brief: The reason scaling has never touched private data is not neglect but definition: a data vendor can only sell what a model is allowed to say back to a user, so the entire commercial data-acquisition layer reproduces the public/private boundary rather than crossing it. That makes the private-corpus problem structurally immune to the industry's current fix for data scarcity — you cannot buy your way past it, because the buying mechanism is what enforces the limit. Any method that works has to spend compute rather than acquire data
data.name: Public data ceiling is structural

data.brief: The right place for a non-deterministic component is precisely the band where the deterministic system is already uncertain — not everywhere, and not nowhere. Static rules degrade because adversaries adapt faster than the rules can be edited; ML scores collapse a rich situation into one number and threshold it; the agent's advantage is that it can be handed real-time, cross-domain context and asked for a reasoned verdict. Keeping tier 1 intact bounds the blast radius, bounds cost, and keeps the latency budget spendable on the few cases that need it.
data.name: Put the non-deterministic component where determinism already fails

data.brief: An emerging language split: training, research, and GPU serving stay Python ("the model ships on pip"), but agents — the new application layer — ship on NPM in TypeScript; the practical edge is one codebase and one consistent type system (a Zod schema defined once, used in agent loop, backend, and UI) versus a Python service + separate typed frontend with a contract to hand-synchronize — Atwood's law extended to agents
data.name: Python is the brain, TypeScript is the body of the agentic application layer

data.brief: The durable claim: AI quality at scale is produced by an organizational loop — trace, sample, annotate with domain expertise, build golden sets, calibrate judges, monitor — in which every function owns a step, and the platform's job is to make each step self-serve (stable APIs, vibe-coded UIs, judge calibration anyone can run). Verification is relocated not only outside the model but outside engineering
data.name: Quality is an org loop not a harness

data.brief: An agent's search behavior is an artifact of its training distribution (code-grep + human-web + BM25-shaped benchmarks), so you cannot fully prompt it away — you reframe the task so the old pattern can't fire ("write one concise sentence describing what you want to find", never "write a search query") and ultimately retrain with rewards that grade query quality itself
data.name: Agent search behavior is a training-distribution artifact you can't prompt away

data.brief: The talk's compressed thesis: "every model has read about your domain, but none has watched the plays and the moves and their outcomes — and that gap is the whole game." A frontier model has read about money; a grounded model has watched what happened. The gap does not close with a bigger model or with more context, because both scale the same input class (descriptions of what people say works); it closes only by adding a different input class — verified outcomes at scale. The uncomfortable corollary for domains without instrumented outcomes is that they cannot buy their way out of the fluent bluff.
data.name: Models have read about your domain but never watched the outcomes

data.brief: Hundreds of trillions of inference tokens a day constitute the largest and most task-relevant distribution in existence, and the industry is spending heavily to manufacture synthetic substitutes for it while that stream goes unused. The bottleneck was never availability but algorithmic: previous methods needed curated tasks, parallel rollouts and replayable environments, none of which production traffic provides. An algorithm requiring only one on-policy rollout and a hint is what makes the real distribution trainable, which is why the method and the trace-mining business model arrive together
data.name: Real token flow is the untapped distribution

data.brief: The central design tension of environments: ambiguity is what makes a task resemble real work (humans never start with complete information, and exploration is the skill being tested), and ambiguity is exactly what multiplies the number of valid solution paths — which makes standardized evaluation "much, much harder". Every realism gain is paid for in grading difficulty, and rubric density is capped by what a judge can apply consistently.
data.name: Every realism gain in an environment is paid for in grading difficulty

data.brief: The talk's one durable idea is the GPS/viewfinder analogy: real-time doesn't make an existing medium faster, it changes what the medium *is* by adding a feedback loop, and each historical instance unlocked a category (ride-hailing, short-form video) invisible from the batch version. If interactive video is genuinely that kind of shift, the applications won't be "better AI video" but new interactive forms — games-that-are-movies, real-time ads, embodied-AI simulators — which is why the infra bet (memory, streaming, global latency) matters more than model quality. The unsolved-evals admission is the honest counterweight
data.name: Realtime is a medium shift not a speedup

data.brief: The most transferable point is that for real-time systems the durable value migrates to the orchestration harness — the GPU/CPU thread management that keeps a stream stutter-free through interrupts and buffering — more than to the model, because the model capability commoditizes while flawless real-time orchestration stays hard. That is the corpus's harness-over-model thesis (claim-1, reliability) confirmed from an entirely different domain, and it predicts that real-time media companies compete on hardness, not on model quality — the same conclusion the CUA and voice-agent talks reached
data.name: Realtime value is in the harness

data.brief: An ontology's value to agents is not just the graph: RDFS/OWL semantics sitting beside it derive facts the graph never stored (domain/range typing, transitive closure) and enforce constraints (functional, disjoint, enumerations) — inference and guardrails from one formalism, applied to LLM output at the point it touches your records.
data.name: RDFS/OWL semantics beside the graph derive facts and enforce constraints

data.brief: More tools only improve local work (better knives, more ovens); autonomous collaboration is a supply-chain problem, and it requires a chain of verifiable receipts proving every step so any result can be trusted downstream. Trust infrastructure — identity, signing, settlement — is the gate to agentic scientific research, not model capability
data.name: Autonomous collaboration needs verifiable receipt chains, not more tools

data.brief: RLMs are the next test-time-compute paradigm because they merge the two prior scaling moves — chain-of-thought/reasoning tokens and (parallel) tool calling — into one mechanism: reasoning BY executing code whose calls include sub-agents/sub-RLMs; whether cognition lives in latent space, reasoning tokens, or code execution is irrelevant next to results
data.name: RLMs merge reasoning tokens and tool calling into one mechanism

data.brief: For generated media reaching real users, layered overlapping gates beat one well-designed gate: a Swiss-cheese arrangement optimizes for the probability that no failure gets all the way through, so redundancy between an in-loop QA agent and a final publish-ready check is the design, not waste. A later gate catching what an earlier one should have caught is a tuning signal for upstream — and rejecting on "unsure", taking a coverage hit rather than publishing, is the correct default when authenticity is the product constraint.
data.name: Layered overlapping gates beat one perfect gate for generated media

data.brief: Execution industrialized out from under the decision: the same refactor now costs 1/5 the effort and will soon zero-shot, so "should we refactor?" has become almost entirely a *judgment* question — weigh compounding tech debt and business ROI against exponentially cheapening future execution, knowing that deferring without guardrails lets AI-velocity recreate the legacy conditions you're deferring escape from. Wisedocs' answer (pause, consolidate, forge ahead) is vindicated in business terms: pipeline time down, costs down, larger files supported, multi-month features shipping in under a week — and the codebase developers *ask* to work in. The talk's closing instruction is literally a call to judgment: "think about the business value of delivering a big refactor and the tradeoffs of doing it now versus in the future"
data.name: Refactor timing is the judgment call

data.brief: Regression-awareness must live inside the optimizer, not after it: fixing failure K+1 in isolation silently trades old wins for new ones, so "no regression on the K past learning environments" has to be a constraint of the optimization itself — and computed sub-linearly in K, or the loop stops being frequently runnable
data.name: Regression-awareness must live inside the optimizer, not after it

data.brief: Absolute quality scores are inter-rater noise; relative comparisons are stable. Ask a room to rate one video 1–10 on storytelling and you get four different numbers; show them two videos and ask which tells the better story and the majority agrees. So build both the training data and the metric on pairs — the model generalizes toward "better", which no amount of rubric-writing gets out of an absolute scale.
data.name: Absolute quality scores are rater noise; relative comparisons are stable

data.brief: Agent reliability is a control-flow problem, not a prompting problem — more prompt rules don't fix mid-run drift/looping; moving state and decisions into a deterministic harness does
data.name: Agent reliability is a control-flow problem, not a prompting problem

data.brief: Evaluate agents like an SRE, not a researcher: reliability, availability, latency, cost, and recovery are the metric set, each mapping to a business outcome (task completion = value delivered, tool success = operational reliability, escalation rate = human burden, safety violations = risk exposure, recovery rate = resilience) — accuracy is deliberately absent from the scorecard because it is an input to dependable outcomes, not the goal
data.name: Evaluate agents like an SRE: reliability metrics, not accuracy, are the scorecard

data.brief: Reliability's near-absence from model-choice criteria (1 in 5) reads not as indifference but as saturation: models are reliable enough, reliability became a threshold requirement, and the real decision moved up the stack to quality, agentic capability, and cost
data.name: Reliability became a threshold requirement; the decision moved up the stack

data.brief: The field's most reliable heuristic, applied to itself: every time a hand-built stage was replaced by a learned one — linguistic features → word vectors, pipeline NLP → end-to-end backpropagation, architecture engineering → learned/unified architectures — results improved. The remaining manual process is the research loop itself, so the highest-leverage move is to have the system build itself. "The best way to build it is to have it built itself".
data.name: Replace the last manual process — the research loop itself

data.brief: "Rent to learn, own to earn" (paraphrase): pre-product-market-fit you can rent intelligence; post-PMF — or when an enterprise budgets a project, which presumes PMF — you cannot afford not to own the inference infrastructure. The rented model's prepaid casino economics (load credits, no monthly anchor) make cost mentally un-anchorable
data.name: Rent to learn, own to earn: own inference after PMF

data.brief: The wrong question is "how do I make the model deterministic"; the right one is "how do I debug and retest a run I can't reproduce." Bitwise determinism is controllability — unobtainable from hosted APIs and undesirable, since sampling variation is what makes the model good; replayability is observability — re-validating a run that already happened, well enough to debug it. Don't freeze the model; capture what it did. You need the same state transition, not the same token
data.name: Ask for replayability, not determinism

data.brief: Invert the incident loop and the human's job changes shape: instead of a person spotting an issue and an agent fixing it, the agent investigates before anyone looks, so you "wake up with an idea of the issues" and evidence already assembled. The honest current state is not autonomy but *cold start* — small fixes land as one-or-two-line PRs, and "the bigger it is the more likely a human's involved in spearheading it over the line", with the human driving steps two and three rather than merely reviewing step one.
data.name: Inverting the incident loop turns the human from responder into reviewer

data.brief: When coding agents make the one-off fix nearly free, the binding constraint moves from writing the code to deciding whether it should exist. Seniority in a forward deployed org is therefore measured in refusals and in generalization — architecting one customer's ask so the next four inherit it — and in front-loaded requirements work that would have been wasted effort when implementation was the expensive step. The failure mode is not slowness but a brittle per-customer black box that neither side can own.
data.name: Seniority in a forward deployed org is measured in refusals and generalization

data.brief: An oracle that hands the model exactly the right memory and still misses the maximum relocates a chunk of the memory problem from retrieval to use: the model can hold the correct evidence and still ignore, misread or be confused by it. Any memory evaluation that stops at retrieval precision is therefore measuring the easier half, and any memory product claiming wins on recall metrics has not yet shown the wins survive to task outcome. The oracle condition is cheap to add and belongs in every memory evaluation as the ceiling estimate it turns out not to be
data.name: Retrieval ceiling is utilization

data.brief: Users only delegate what they believe they can take back: keep level-2 self-serve features alongside agents, let users pause the belt, fix, and restart ("take the wheel, not abandon the car"), and present approvable plans before irreversible actions (e.g. data entry that can erase tax-software records) — reversibility is the trust substrate that makes delegation happen at all
data.name: Users only delegate what they believe they can take back

data.brief: Abolishing code review did not abolish review — it relocated it to where humans still add signal: design docs (broadcast, and mandatory to have readers), architectural invariants (asserted once, enforced by CI forever), and triage of agent-found issues into real / hallucinated / tasteless. The counterintuitive result is more process, not less, and the analogy offered is CI itself: teams that refused it because "it would slow us down" did slow down for three months and then moved much faster. "Our processes have to evolve if we're going to ship at agent speed" — the cost of the new process is paid up front, in the same shape as the old one.
data.name: Abolishing code review relocated review rather than removing it

data.brief: The scarce resource governing an agent loop is human review capacity, not tokens or compute. If nobody has reviewed the loop's last PR, another iteration only manufactures work nobody wants — so the loop should read its own labels and refuse to run.
data.description: Scaling then happens along axes that respect that constraint: batch 3-5 items per run with a separate implementation phase (and context window) each — cheaper and more reliable — or run the workflow N times and hand one PR to each of N teammates, rather than letting one loop stack N PRs on one reviewer.
data.name: Human review capacity, not tokens, is the scarce resource governing a loop

data.brief: When generation industrializes, the scarce reviewing resource stops being code-reading capacity and becomes decision-alignment capacity. Post-hoc review of an agent-authored PR flood cannot answer "what matters here?" fast enough; moving review to the decision point — shared plans aligned before anyone (human or agent) spends a day building — converts unreviewable output back into simple reviews, and catches direction-divergence before it costs a prototype. Verification is re-architected *earlier in the pipeline* rather than scaled at the end
data.name: Review moves to the decision point

data.brief: The talk's sharpest point is that automating review's correctness function does not eliminate review — it strips it down to its actual purpose, alignment, which is a human coordination problem no verifier replaces. Teams that read "AI reviews everything" as "no one reviews" have thrown away the alignment that made review valuable; teams that relocate the human to owning architecture and intent keep it. That reframes the whole kill-the-review debate as a question of *which half you automate*, and it is the same execution-industrializes-judgment-survives shape as pat-value-of-judgement, here specific to collaboration
data.name: Review value migrates to alignment

data.brief: Why continual learning is stuck: not model capability but the abstraction level of environment and reward design, which is still where coding was before agents. The prescription mirrors what happened to coding — move up a level and let compute do the refining (mine your own deployment, calibrate difficulty, extract rubrics, validate by training), so environment design becomes something a practitioner does rather than a research project. The closing loop is the payoff: models stay in the guardrails, find the issues in production, and those issues become the next tasks.
data.name: Continual learning is stuck on the abstraction level of environment and reward design

data.brief: Pouring millions into one-off AI vuln discovery in open-source libraries is whack-a-mole; a one-time rewrite of critical libraries into memory-safe languages gives programmatic guarantees that hold even as attack models get smarter — spend defender-AI capacity on fundamental controls, not patches
data.name: Memory-safe rewrites beat whack-a-mole AI vulnerability discovery

data.brief: "Should I still read code?" is the wrong question; the right one is "what proof does this specific change need?" The continuum sorts tasks, not people: the same engineer YOLOs a non-critical change and line-reads auth/money/permissions/irreversible-data code the same afternoon. Reading spends attention once; engineering the system (docs, linters, reviewer memory, rails, observability, rollback) makes the catch permanent — inspect the system for repeated mistake classes, inspect the lines only where blast radius demands it
data.name: The right question is what proof does this specific change need

data.brief: Routing is evolving from per-prompt model picking into a persistent session-level controller — and the panel argues the controller is structural: applications built on non-deterministic components "operate in a very low-trust environment," no participant has a perfectly visible world, so "there will have to be some form of arbitration… at the orchestration level," with the web's history as precedent (traffic-based routing controls centralized over time). The open question the panel splits on is *where* it lives — product, plumbing, or the models themselves — with the closing synthesis that "there's not going to be a really great harness in absence of a really great model and vice versa"
data.name: Routing centralizes into a controller

data.brief: Split remediation agents into three concerns with different trust models: deterministic rules for directly observable facts (schema drift, rate thresholds, error families — explicit rules are easier to validate); a small learned policy only for bounded contextual action selection; and safety guards with final authority placed OUTSIDE the learned policy — so no policy update can silently redefine its own authority. Rules for facts, learning for bounded choices, guards for authority
data.name: Rules for facts, learning for bounded choices, guards for authority

data.brief: Runtime LLMs turn the model from a build-time asset generator into a live game director — but the technology itself does not make the product better; with polish democratized and every studio exploring the same tech, the scarce input is taste: the feel for which subset of humans will find a game fun and why. How to use runtime LLMs to differentiate is still unsolved, industry-wide, at day zero
data.name: Runtime LLMs make the model a live game director; taste is the scarce input

data.brief: Agent capability and agent safety are the same design problem, solved in the harness: the goal is just enough capability to act autonomously without destructive reach — approval handlers where humans must stay in the loop, argument-locking (partial function application) where they shouldn't have to be; none of it lives in the model
data.name: Agent capability and agent safety are the same design problem, solved in the harness

data.brief: From running always-on personal agents: attempts to instruction-tame agents "don't work"; the only reliable control is structural — sandbox them so harm is impossible ("our brains can't stop the heart at will") and mediate anything that changes state. Locking down after the fact (the OpenClaw path) costs most of the usefulness — so build the cage before the wildness, not around it
data.name: Taming agents by instruction fails; only structural sandboxing controls them

data.brief: Every method in this space can be made to look good on a single pass and they differ only in where they stop, so the honest evaluation is not "does it learn D" but "does adding compute keep helping." Under that test the field's current toolkit is uniformly bounded, and the one existence proof of an unbounded curve — self-play — worked because improvement fed back into problem difficulty. The practical filter for anyone assessing continual-learning vendors is therefore to ask what happens on the second and third pass, not the first
data.name: Saturation is the real benchmark

data.brief: The argument that makes this more than an equity talk: if the dominant axis of progress required co-located capital-intensive compute, then participation was decided by balance sheets regardless of ideas — and if that axis has saturated, the redistribution follows mechanically rather than as a favour. Post-training and agentic compute are distributable, higher-return per FLOP, and purchasable in different quantities, so the field's competitive question shifts from who can hoard GPUs to who has the better recipe. That is a falsifiable claim about compute economics, and it is what a new architecture would reverse
data.name: Saturation redistributes participation

data.brief: The hierarchy scaffold is the same kind of trick chain-of-thought was on GPT-4-era models: a harness compensating for missing post-training. As models get better at compartmentalizing problems natively, these tricks should be needed less and less — harness value at this layer is expected to erode
data.name: Hierarchy scaffolds are transitional tricks like chain-of-thought

data.brief: Hardware scaling is near its floor: fp32→fp4 numerical precision delivered ~32x (transistor cost ≈ exponent + mantissa², so shrinking mantissas compounds) while raw hardware gave ~3x, and there is no "fp0" next step; the capability curve continued only because of an algorithmic paradigm (reasoning halved the doubling time from ~7 to ~3.5 months post-o1) — future gains come from algorithms (FlashAttention lineage, MTP/DeepSpark 2–6x, gradient checkpointing, diffusion LMs), which is also why Han doubts standalone ASIC companies
data.name: Hardware scaling is near its floor; future gains come from algorithms

data.brief: The payoff of a graph comes from discipline at extraction time — schema, ontology instructions, embedding-based entity matching — not from the database. Free-form triple extraction produces a graph you "wouldn't get very far with"; typed structure is what makes relationships meaningful and queryable
data.name: Graph payoff comes from extraction-time discipline, not the database

data.brief: The two principles are a product, not a sum: scoping without an agent factory loses to agent-native competitors on speed; an agent factory without scoping industrializes building the wrong thing. Automating an unexamined intake pipeline does not produce leverage, it produces volume — the same failure the iOS/Android story produced by hand, at machine scale. Which is why Ramp put its first agent on the scoping stage rather than the implementation stage.
data.name: Scoping discipline and the agent factory multiply rather than add
